docs.text:
Cross-cutting ideas, trends, and frameworks in market research:

These environments afford opportunities for shallow skilling while restricting fuller development of capacities, with significant implications for AI's impact on human flourishing. capacity-conducive-environments 2026-07-03 2026-07-22 Environments that actively encourage the development and exercise of human capacities through rich opportunities for embodied interaction and shared valuing, providing alternatives to capacity-hostile conditions. These environments afford structured and unstructured embodied interactions necessary for intersubjective habituation of capacities. agential-control 2026-07-03 2026-07-25 The ability to adjust the execution of an action as the performance unfolds, a key component of being skilled that distinguishes skills from habits, as detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. Skills require control over initiating the task, whereas habits are merely triggered by environmental cues. habituation-process 2026-07-03 2026-07-25 The gradual process of becoming skilled through practice, involving inculcation through continued attunement to demands of individual cases, with critical implications for AI's impact on skill development. Skill development cannot be learned through testimony alone but requires practice, encountering and overcoming disappointment and failure. intersubjectivity-in-skilling 2026-07-03 2026-07-22 The shared understanding dimension of skill development, where learning occurs through relationships with others who guide and share the value of the skill. Becoming skilled typically requires a mentor to instill not only mechanical aspects but also the value of the skill. embodiment-in-skilling 2026-07-03 2026-07-22 The essential role of physical presence and sensory experience in the development of human capacities, particularly social and moral skills. Embodied interaction is critical for recognizing others as moral agents and forming meaningful relationships. ai-deskilling-structural-problem 2026-07-03 2026-07-22 The phenomenon where AI systems undermine human capacities through systemic conditions that create environments hostile to capacity cultivation, as established in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. This should be understood as a structural problem requiring societal solutions, not merely an individual responsibility issue. ai-adoption-selection-bias 2026-07-03 2026-07-10 The substantial pre-existing differences between AI adopters and non-adopters that complicate causal inference in AI impact studies. ai-adoption-methodological-innovation 2026-07-03 2026-07-10 Methodological advances in measuring AI adoption, particularly the shift from occupational exposure scores to direct firm-level spending data. methodological-heterogeneity-in-ai-studies 2026-07-03 2026-07-10 The challenge that different AI adoption measurement approaches yield dramatically different findings about AI's economic impact. pepm-metric 2026-07-15 2026-07-15 PEPM (AI Spend Per Employee) metric measures the intensity of AI adoption at the firm level by calculating monthly AI vendor spend per employee over the first three months after sustained adoption begins. ai-adoption-intensity-terciles 2026-07-15 2026-07-15 Methodology categorizing firms based on AI adoption intensity, dividing them into high (top tercile) and low (bottom two terciles) intensity groups based on PEPM metric. developmental-perfectionism 2026-07-15 2026-07-22 Neo-Aristotelian approach to human flourishing where flourishing is understood as a complex, unified, and well-rounded life, providing the philosophical foundation for understanding why capacity-deskilling is harmful. human-capacities 2026-07-15 2026-07-22 Core abilities that constitute human flourishing, including epistemic, social, creative, and volitional capacities, which are fundamental to being human and can be undermined by AI systems. plan-forming-vs-plan-following 2026-07-17 2026-07-25 The distinction between actively creating plans through self-deliberation (requiring agential control) versus executing pre-determined plans (more habitual), with critical implications for AI's impact on capacity development as analyzed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. narrow-field-of-affordances 2026-07-17 2026-07-22 An environment that provides limited action possibilities, restricting opportunities for the development and exercise of human capacities, a key mechanism through which AI systems can create capacity-hostile environments as detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. epistemic-capacities 2026-07-18 2026-07-22 The human capacities related to knowledge, reasoning, and understanding, including theoretical rationality and practical rationality (phronesis), which are essential for navigating truth and making informed decisions. social-capacities 2026-07-18 2026-07-22 The human capacities related to forming meaningful relationships, understanding others' perspectives, and participating in communal life, including moral capacity and relational capacity. creative-capacities 2026-07-18 2026-07-22 The human capacities related to generating novel ideas, making unfamiliar combinations of familiar concepts, and transforming conceptual spaces, which enable innovation and adaptation. volitional-capacity 2026-07-18 2026-07-22 The human capacity to exert effort, overcome difficulty, persevere, and grow in order to achieve intrinsically valuable goals, treated as a meta-capacity necessary for developing all other capacities. plan-following 2026-07-25 2026-07-25 Plan-following refers to the execution of pre-determined plans without exercising agential control over the planning process itself. As analyzed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, this represents a habitual mode of action where individuals respond to environmental triggers rather than initiating and adjusting plans through self-deliberation.

docs.text:
Key research studies and reports:

Page First Observed Last Updated Description pwc-2026-global-ai-jobs-barometer 2026-06-25 2026-06-27 PwC's comprehensive analysis of over one billion job advertisements examining AI's impact on the global labor market. mrii-2026-market-research-study 2026-06-28 2026-06-28 The Market Research Institute International 2026 global study represents the fourth annual comprehensive analysis of market research and insights professionals worldwide. burning-glass-beyond-binary 2026-06-28 2026-06-28 Published in January 2026 by the Burning Glass Institute, "Beyond the Binary" represents a landmark analysis challenging the conventional wisdom that AI will either automate or augment jobs. ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study 2026-07-03 2026-07-15 A comprehensive analysis of how AI adoption affects employment patterns across 21,559 firms, using observed AI spending data linked to workforce records. Shows high-intensity adopters grow headcount by 10.2% and entry-level roles by 12.0%. ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem 2026-07-10 2026-07-25 Avigail Ferdman's 2026 paper in AI & Society presenting a structural analysis of how AI systems can undermine human capacities through systemic environmental conditions rather than individual failings. Introduces the critical distinction between capacity-hostile and capacity-conducive environments, analyzes the role of agential control and habituation in capacity development, and examines how Artificial Personal Assistants may create capacity-hostile environments by encouraging plan-following rather than plan-forming. The paper argues that deskilling should be understood as a structural problem requiring societal solutions rather than merely an individual responsibility issue.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The ability to adjust the execution of an action as the performance unfolds, a key component of being skilled that distinguishes skills from habits, as detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. Skills require control over initiating the task, whereas habits are merely triggered by environmental cues.

docs.title: Philosophical Foundation
docs.text: Ferdman draws on skill philosophy to establish that: - To be skilled in something is to have agential control over it - As agency develops, the balance between automaticity and control shifts through tuning and attuning - Skilled agents develop flexible links between thought and action that continue to evolve even after expertise is achieved - Skills are distinct from habits: skills require control over initiating the task, while habits are elicited in response to environmental triggers

docs.title: Plan-Forming vs. Plan-Following
docs.text:
Agential control is central to the distinction between: - Plan-forming: Actively creating plans through self-deliberation, requiring control over both settling (deciding between options) and coordinating functions of planning - Plan-following: Executing pre-determined plans without exercising agential control over the planning process itself

As Ferdman explains, 'forming a plan by self-deliberation requires exercising control over all the steps of the activity of forming the plan,' whereas 'relying on an APA to form our plans for us is more like a habit that is developed in response to a trigger in the environment.'

docs.title: Implications for AI Adoption
docs.text: In market research contexts, agential control is threatened when: - AI tools automate routine analytical tasks that researchers previously used to develop judgment - Systems provide recommendations without requiring researchers to justify conclusions - Platforms offload client interaction to chatbots, reducing opportunities for embodied relationship building - Decision-support tools present outputs as definitive rather than as prompts for deliberation

docs.title: Maintaining Agential Control
docs.text: Strategies to preserve agential control in AI-augmented research: - Design workflows where researchers must explain and justify AI-generated insights - Create 'red team' processes where alternative interpretations are deliberately sought - Structure projects to maintain human oversight of critical decision points - Ensure AI tools support rather than replace the planning process - Develop training that emphasizes the researcher's role as the ultimate decision-maker

docs.title: Connection to Capacity Development
docs.text:
Agential control is essential for: - Developing practical wisdom through real-world experience - Taking responsibility for outcomes to enable self-critique and improvement - Exercising the volitional capacity to overcome difficulty and grow - Engaging in the habituation process necessary for skill development

Without agential control, researchers risk becoming plan-followers rather than plan-formers, diminishing their capacity for independent judgment and creative problem-solving.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: AI Adoption Intensity Terciles is a methodology developed in the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study to categorize firms based on the intensity of their AI adoption, measured by the PEPM (AI Spend Per Employee) metric.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
1. Firms are classified as AI adopters when they have three consecutive months of at least $100 in AI vendor spending
  2. Adoption intensity is measured as monthly AI spend per employee (PEPM) over the first three months after adoption
  3. Among treated firms, PEPM values are sorted and divided into three equal groups (terciles):
  4. High intensity: top tercile (most intensive AI adopters)
  5. Medium intensity: middle tercile
  6. Low intensity: bottom tercile (least intensive AI adopters)
  7. For analysis, firms are often grouped as:
  8. High intensity: top tercile
  9. Low intensity: bottom two terciles combined

docs.title: Rationale for Tercile Approach
docs.text:
• Allows researchers to examine differential impacts of AI adoption based on intensity
  • Reveals that not all AI adopters experience the same employment effects
  • Helps address selection bias by comparing firms with similar eventual adoption intensity
  • Shows that substantial employment gains are concentrated among high-intensity adopters

docs.title: Key Findings Using Intensity Terciles
docs.text:
• High-intensity adopters grew total employment by 10.2% following adoption
  • Entry-level headcount rose 12.0% for high-intensity adopters
  • Low-intensity adopters showed no statistically significant change in employment
  • High-intensity gains emerged gradually over 18-24 months, suggesting a learning curve
  • Employment gains were broad across roles for high-intensity adopters (engineering, sales, administration, customer service)

docs.title: Significance
docs.text: This methodology revealed a critical insight often missed in prior research: AI's labor market effects differ substantially based on adoption intensity. Studies that treat all adopters the same may miss these nuanced patterns.

docs.text: Methodological advances in measuring AI adoption, particularly the shift from occupational exposure scores to direct firm-level spending data. The ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study represents a breakthrough in this area by using observed AI vendor payments rather than theoretical exposure metrics.

docs.title: Ramp-Revelio Methodology
docs.text:
The study introduces the AI Spend Per Employee Methodology (PEPM):

  1. Adoption definition: Three consecutive months of ≥$100 AI vendor spend
  2. Intensity measure: PEPM = (sum of first 3 months' AI spend) / (3 × baseline headcount)
  3. Intensity stratification: Low (bottom two PEPM terciles), High (top PEPM tercile)
  4. Comparison design: Later adopters within same intensity group

This approach overcomes four critical limitations of prior methods:

  1. Direct observation: Measures actual adoption behavior rather than theoretical exposure
  2. Timing precision: Captures exact adoption month rather than imputed timing
  3. Intensity dimension: Reveals differential effects by adoption intensity
  4. Firm-level specificity: Avoids occupational aggregation that masks firm differences

docs.title: Observed Spending Threshold
docs.text: The $100/month threshold excludes one-off experiments while capturing sustained adoption, addressing the "Is this really AI adoption?" question that plagues survey-based approaches.

docs.title: PEPM Metric
docs.text: Using baseline headcount in the denominator makes intensity comparable across firm sizes and keeps employee scale predetermined relative to adoption timing.

docs.title: Staggered Treatment Design
docs.text: The Callaway-Sant'Anna framework accounts for heterogeneous treatment timing, avoiding biases in traditional event-study approaches.

docs.title: Evidence of Impact
docs.text: This methodological innovation revealed findings invisible to exposure-based studies: - Only high-intensity adopters (+10.2% headcount growth) showed significant employment effects - Entry-level roles grew 12.0% among high-intensity adopters, contradicting exposure-based predictions - Effects concentrated in Information sector (+13.4% growth), not uniformly distributed

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
This methodological shift has critical implications:

  • Vendor evaluation: Must measure actual usage intensity, not just adoption status
  • Impact assessment: Requires tracking spending patterns over time, not binary adoption
  • Benchmarking: Industry comparisons must account for intensity differences
  • ROI calculation: Benefits appear only above critical intensity thresholds

docs.title: Cross-References
docs.text: This innovation directly addresses the ai-adoption-selection-bias problem and explains the methodological-heterogeneity-in-ai-studies observed across research. It represents a critical advance over the pwc-ai-occupational-exposure-index used in pwc-2026-global-ai-jobs-barometer.

docs.title: Practical Implementation
docs.text:
For market research organizations, adopting this methodological innovation means: - Tracking actual AI spending rather than adoption claims - Measuring intensity through normalized spending metrics - Comparing against firms with similar pre-adoption characteristics - Focusing on sustained usage patterns rather than initial adoption

Without these methodological improvements, organizations risk misattributing effects or missing the intensity threshold needed for positive returns—precisely what the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study demonstrates.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The substantial pre-existing differences between AI adopters and non-adopters that complicate causal inference in AI impact studies. As rigorously documented in the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study, these selection effects mean AI adopters were already distinct from non-adopters before AI adoption, creating significant methodological challenges.

docs.title: Key Evidence
docs.text:
The Ramp-Revelio study demonstrates dramatic pre-adoption differences:

Characteristic AI Adopters Never Adopters Difference Headcount (mean) 144.2 103.9 +40.3* Engineering share 26.8% 18.6% +8.2* Entry-level share 42.1% 50.4% -8.3* YoY growth (median) 6.0% 1.6% +4.4* Mean salary $110,346 $93,847 +$16,499* Tech-adjacent sector 54.2% 25.9% +28.3* VC-backed 34.0% 9.5% +24.5*

*Statistically significant at p<0.01

docs.title: Methodological Implications
docs.text:
This selection bias creates three critical challenges for AI impact research:

  1. Confounded comparisons: Simple adopter vs. non-adopter comparisons conflate AI effects with pre-existing differences
  2. Pre-trend divergence: Adopters were already on different growth trajectories before adoption (see Figure 4 in Ramp-Revelio study)
  3. Sector concentration: AI adoption heavily concentrated in Information (53.7%), Finance (43.6%), and Professional Services (36.0%)

docs.title: Addressing the Bias
docs.text:
The Ramp-Revelio study employs sophisticated methods to address selection bias:

  • Preferred comparison: Later adopters within the same eventual intensity group
  • Sector fixed effects: Controlling for industry composition differences
  • Event-time analysis: Tracking pre-treatment parallel trends
  • Intensity stratification: Separating low vs. high adoption intensity effects

This approach revealed that only high-intensity adopters (top PEPM tercile) showed significant employment growth (+10.2%), while low-intensity adopters showed no significant change.

docs.title: Contrast with Exposure-Based Studies
docs.text: This selection bias explains why exposure-based studies (like pwc-2026-global-ai-jobs-barometer) often produce different findings than spending-based studies: - Exposure scores cannot distinguish firms that adopt AI from those that don't - They assume uniform adoption effects across firms with identical workforce composition - They miss the critical intensity dimension revealed by actual spending data

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
This concept has profound implications for insights organizations:

  • Vendor selection: AI tools adopted by leading firms may reflect pre-existing advantages rather than causal benefits
  • Implementation strategy: Success depends on organizational readiness, not just tool adoption
  • Impact measurement: Must account for pre-existing differences when evaluating AI initiatives
  • Benchmarking: Comparing against industry averages without controlling for selection effects is misleading

docs.title: Cross-References
docs.text: This concept is central to understanding the methodological-heterogeneity-in-ai-studies problem and represents a key ai-adoption-methodological-innovation addressed by the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study. It explains why the employment gains documented in that study are concentrated among high-intensity adopters in specific sectors, rather than across all AI adopters.

docs.title: Practical Guidance
docs.text:
For market research professionals, addressing selection bias requires: - Never comparing AI adopters to non-adopters without controlling for pre-existing differences - Measuring adoption intensity (PEPM) rather than binary adoption status - Using staggered adoption timing in evaluation designs - Focusing on high-intensity implementation for meaningful impact

Without these precautions, organizations risk attributing pre-existing advantages to AI adoption or missing the intensity threshold needed for positive returns.

docs.title: Ai democratization
docs.text: AI democratization refers to the process where AI automates more expert tasks, leaving less expert tasks for humans.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: AI democratization describes how artificial intelligence makes advanced capabilities accessible by automating complex expert tasks, thereby reducing expertise requirements for certain occupations. As quantified in Figure 2 of the PwC 2026 report, this process affects 52% of global job postings. Concrete examples include [[recruiters]] (AI automates CV screening while humans handle contract negotiation) and [[inventory-clerks]] (AI manages stock optimization while humans perform physical movement). Figure 3 demonstrates democratization is particularly strong in high AI exposure jobs, where expertise requirements decrease significantly. Crucially, Figure 11 reveals that despite reduced expertise demands, democratized roles maintain high epoch-score (0.48), indicating continued reliance on human capabilities for remaining tasks—often involving physical dexterity, adaptability, or interpersonal skills. The report warns that while democratization expands job accessibility (e.g., enabling non-experts to perform data analysis), it may compress career ladders and reduce skill development opportunities without targeted interventions. This concept represents one of two primary pathways (alongside ai-professionalization) in AI's labor market restructuring. Organizations can leverage democratization through the ai-job-future-framework's 'Supply and Demand' dimension, redesigning roles to balance AI efficiency with human execution. The trend is accelerating post-2022, as shown in Figure 9's widening skill transformation gap, requiring proactive workforce planning to ensure equitable access to emerging opportunities in democratized roles.

docs.title: AI Deskilling as a Structural Problem
Definition
docs.text: The phenomenon where AI systems undermine human capacities through systemic conditions that create environments hostile to capacity cultivation, as established in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. This should be understood as a structural problem requiring societal solutions, not merely an individual responsibility issue.

docs.title: Core Argument
docs.text: Ferdman challenges the individual responsibility framework for addressing AI-induced deskilling, arguing that: - Deskilling results from structural conditions rather than individual failings - We develop and exercise capacities in response to our social and material environment - Deficient environments lead to capacity impoverishment and subsequent devaluation - Expecting individuals to 'will themselves' to resist deskilling overlooks crucial structural aspects

docs.title: Capacity Impoverishment
docs.text: The deskilling of core human capacities is harmful because: - Inadequate development of capacities diminishes us as humans - Capacity impoverishment undermines our flourishing - Unlike skill obsolescence (e.g., hunting, basket-weaving), capacity deskilling should always be a cause for worry - Impoverished capacities lead to impoverished lives

docs.title: Structural Dimensions
docs.text: The paper identifies three key structural dimensions of capacity deskilling:

docs.title: 1. Narrow Field of Affordances
docs.text:
• AI systems create environments with restricted action possibilities
  • Automation reduces opportunities to practice judgment and strengthen 'cognitive musculature'
  • Cumulative effect of automation across multiple spheres creates capacity-hostile conditions

docs.title: 2. Diminished Embodiment
docs.text:
• Digital interfaces reduce opportunities for embodied interaction
  • Disembodied environments make it harder to form meaningful relationships
  • Without physical presence, recognizing others as moral agents requires more mental effort

docs.title: 3. Erosion of Intersubjectivity
docs.text:
• AI tools replace human mentors with algorithmic guidance
  • Reduced opportunities for shared valuing of capacities
  • Diminished transmission of tacit knowledge through apprenticeship

docs.title: Artificial Personal Assistants Case Study
docs.text: Ferdman analyzes how AI-powered personal assistants threaten capacity development by: - Encouraging plan-following rather than plan-forming - Replacing self-deliberation with automated recommendations - Diminishing practical wisdom development through reduced real-world experience - Creating environments where users respond to AI outputs as environmental triggers

docs.title: Market Research Implications
docs.text: This structural perspective explains: - The entry-level squeeze as AI eliminates routine tasks that served as training grounds - The human operating model gap as a systemic issue rather than individual skill deficiency - Why high-intensity AI adopters must intentionally design capacity-conducive environments - The limitations of technical upskilling without addressing structural conditions

docs.title: Societal Solutions
docs.text: Ferdman calls for: - Critical reflection on values inherent in AI socio-technical systems - Societal obligation to foster capacity-conducive environments - Design of public goods that encourage embodied interaction - Structural interventions rather than individual responsibility frameworks

docs.title: Contrast with Individual Responsibility Approach
docs.text: Unlike approaches that expect individuals to 'be virtuous superheroes' and will themselves to cultivate capacities, the structural perspective: - Recognizes environmental constraints on capacity development - Identifies systemic conditions that create capacity-hostile environments - Calls for societal solutions rather than individual willpower - Focuses on designing environments conducive to human flourishing

docs.title: Ai job future framework
docs.text: A framework of four questions to analyze how AI is reshaping specific occupations, developed by PwC in their 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: The AI Job Future Framework, introduced in Figure 6 of PwC's 2026 report, provides a structured methodology to assess AI's occupational impact through four critical questions: (1) Expertise: How is AI changing required human expertise? (e.g., democratization reduces expertise needs while professionalization increases them); (2) Supply and Demand: How might job demand and worker supply shift as AI reshapes roles?; (3) AI's limitations: Where is human oversight needed for quality control or atypical cases?; and (4) Environmental forces: How do regulations, business bottlenecks, or ethics constrain AI adoption? The report demonstrates the framework's application across diverse occupations: For [[pharmacists]], AI handles prescription processing (Expertise shift) but humans manage patient counseling (AI's limitations); for [[software-developers]], AI generates code but humans focus on architecture (Environmental forces). Figure 9 validates the framework by showing how high AI exposure roles undergo 2.2x faster skill changes, directly addressing the Supply and Demand dimension. Organizations using this tool can anticipate skill shifts, redesign roles, and develop targeted training—particularly valuable for navigating the 'superstar effect' (Figure 12). The framework also explains wage dynamics: roles requiring human oversight of AI (Question 3) command higher premiums, as seen in Figure 15's 62% average AI skill premium. By systematically addressing these questions, employers can transform AI disruption into opportunity, while workers identify future-proof career paths in the evolving labor market. This methodology has become essential for strategic workforce planning in the AI era.

docs.title: New Evidence and Refinement
docs.text:
The mrii-2026-market-research-study provides compelling evidence of AI professionalization in the insights industry: - As AI handles routine analytical tasks, value is shifting upstream toward strategic functions - Insights teams must evolve from delivering answers to shaping decisions, driving growth, and influencing strategy - Pam Forbus of [[mondelez]] states: "AI will increasingly answer questions, deliver insights, execute projects, and support stakeholders faster and at lower cost than ever before. That doesn't diminish the role of insights teams; it fundamentally changes it."

This represents a specific manifestation of professionalization where AI automation of basic tasks elevates the importance of strategic human capabilities.

The value-chain-shift concept further explains this dynamic - as AI makes answers faster and cheaper, the answers themselves become less differentiated, pushing value creation toward higher-order strategic functions.

docs.title: Relationship to Skills Development
docs.text:
A critical finding from the MRII study reveals a professionalization paradox: - Professionals prioritize learning technical AI skills - Leaders value business acumen, communication, and strategic influence more highly

This disconnect threatens to undermine the professionalization process, as organizations may automate tasks without adequately developing the human capabilities needed for the elevated roles.

docs.text: The burning-glass-beyond-binary report shows that professionalization occurs alongside automation within the same occupations. This creates particular challenges for entry-level positions through the entry-level-squeeze, as foundational tasks that build expertise are automated before new developmental pathways are established.

docs.title: Organizational Implications
docs.text: Successful navigation of AI professionalization requires: - Redesigning roles to preserve meaningful human involvement in value-creating activities - Developing new apprenticeship models that build expertise despite automated foundational tasks - Aligning skill development priorities with the evolving value chain

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Environments that actively encourage the development and exercise of human capacities through rich opportunities for embodied interaction and shared valuing, providing alternatives to capacity-hostile conditions as detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. These environments afford structured and unstructured embodied interactions necessary for intersubjective habituation of capacities.

docs.title: Embodied Interaction
docs.text: Capacity-conducive environments prioritize physical presence that enables: - 'Participatory sense-making' where meaning is generated through the interplay between unfolding interaction and participants - Recognition of others as embodied moral agents through voice and gaze - Development of moral attention through embodied understanding - Formation of meaningful relationships that cannot be achieved through disembodied interaction

docs.title: Intersubjective Habituation
docs.text: These environments facilitate capacity development through: - Mentor-mentee relationships where shared valuing of capacities is cultivated - Social practices that generate moral reasons for action through constitutive aims - Community settings that provide opportunities for shared experiences - Public goods like community centers, libraries, and quality public spaces

docs.title: Agential Control Support
docs.text: They encourage users to exercise control over: - Initiating activities rather than merely responding to environmental triggers - Self-deliberation in planning and decision-making - Adjusting execution of actions as performance unfolds - Taking responsibility for outcomes to enable self-critique and improvement

docs.title: Examples in Market Research
docs.text:
• Research environments where junior analysts work alongside senior colleagues on complex projects
  • Client workshops that require embodied interaction and real-time adaptation
  • Training programs that scaffold skill development through graduated responsibility
  • Communities of practice where researchers share insights and develop shared understanding
  • Tools that augment rather than replace human judgment, requiring researchers to justify AI suggestions

docs.title: Contrast with Capacity-Hostile Environments
docs.text: Unlike capacity-hostile-environments, which create narrow fields of affordances, capacity-conducive environments: - Provide sufficient invitations for valuable activities that trigger capacity development - Encourage (not just afford) engagement in activities that develop multiple capacities simultaneously - Support the development of practical wisdom through real-world experience - Foster environments where users become plan-formers rather than plan-followers

docs.title: Implementation Strategies
docs.text: To create capacity-conducive environments in AI-augmented research: - Design AI tools that require researchers to explain and justify AI-generated insights - Structure workflows that maintain human oversight of critical decision points - Create opportunities for embodied client interaction even when using AI tools - Develop mentorship programs that explicitly cultivate shared valuing of research capacities - Ensure AI adoption doesn't eliminate the routine tasks necessary for habituation

docs.title: Connection to Human Flourishing
docs.text: These environments support the neo-Aristotelian concept of developmental-perfectionism, where flourishing is understood as a complex, unified, and well-rounded life achieved through competent exercise of human capacities.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Environments that restrict, limit, or create a narrow field of affordances for the development and exercise of core human capacities, as analyzed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. These environments afford opportunities for shallow skilling while restricting fuller development of capacities, with significant implications for AI's impact on human flourishing.

docs.title: Narrow Field of Affordances
docs.text: Capacity-hostile environments provide limited action possibilities that systematically restrict opportunities for capacity development. As Ferdman explains, these environments: - Create 'affordance shrinkage' that is systematic, enduring, and deeply entrenched - Fail to encourage (not just afford) valuable activities that trigger capacity development - Discourage users from finding compensatory pathways due to the cumulative effect of automation

docs.title: Automation Bias
docs.text: These environments often encourage over-reliance on AI systems through: - Offloading critical tasks to machines (e.g., diagnostic reasoning in healthcare) - Replacing routine activities that are essential for habituation ('depriving users of routine opportunities to practice their judgment and strengthen their cognitive musculature') - Creating contexts where users respond to AI outputs as environmental triggers rather than exercising agential control

docs.title: Disembodiment
docs.text: Many capacity-hostile environments feature: - Reduced embodied interaction that undermines moral attention - Diminished opportunities for recognizing others as moral agents - Limited shared experiences necessary for intersubjective habituation

docs.title: Examples in Market Research
docs.text:
• AI tools that automate foundational research tasks without providing scaffolding for skill development
  • Platforms that replace human interaction in client relationships with chatbots
  • Systems that offload analytical reasoning to AI without requiring researchers to justify conclusions
  • Tools that generate research reports without requiring researchers to engage in the planning process

docs.title: Contrast with Capacity-Conducive Environments
docs.text: Unlike capacity-conducive-environments, which actively encourage embodied interaction and shared valuing, capacity-hostile environments: - Restrict opportunities for developing agential control - Undermine the habituation process through automation - Diminish intersubjectivity in skilling by reducing human interaction - Create conditions where users become plan-followers rather than plan-formers

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: Understanding capacity-hostile environments explains the structural nature of the human-operating-model-gap and why the entry-level-squeeze occurs - traditional entry-level positions increasingly fail to provide the affordances necessary for developing professional capacities through habituation.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The human capacities related to generating novel ideas, making unfamiliar combinations of familiar concepts, and transforming conceptual spaces, which enable innovation and adaptation. As detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, these capacities are constitutive of human flourishing and can be undermined by AI systems.

docs.title: Novel Idea Generation
docs.text:
• Creating ideas that are genuinely new rather than merely recombining existing elements
  • Going beyond what is mechanically possible to produce truly innovative concepts
  • Transforming conceptual spaces rather than operating within established frameworks

docs.title: Unfamiliar Combinations
docs.text:
• Making connections between seemingly unrelated concepts
  • Breaking free from conventional patterns of thought
  • Creating syntheses that reveal new possibilities and perspectives

docs.title: Transformation of Conceptual Spaces
docs.text:
• Changing the framework within which problems are understood
  • Creating new categories and ways of thinking
  • Enabling paradigm shifts rather than incremental improvements

docs.title: Role in Planning and Adaptation
docs.text: Creative capacities are essential for effective planning: - Planning is 'always incomplete, and executing the plan requires the ability to reconsider and respond to novel situations, surprises and unexpected events' - Creative adaptation is necessary when encountering unexpected circumstances - Innovation in methodology and approach drives research excellence - Transformative thinking enables researchers to see beyond conventional interpretations

docs.title: AI's Threat to Creative Capacities
docs.text: Ferdman identifies how AI systems undermine creative capacities: - Providing pre-determined recommendations that reduce opportunities for novel idea generation - Creating environments where users 'respond to the APA's recommendations' rather than initiating creative processes - Automating routine tasks that previously served as foundations for creative development - Diminishing opportunities to encounter and overcome disappointment and failure, which are essential for creative growth

docs.title: Research Design
docs.text:
• AI tools that generate standardized research approaches without opportunities for innovation
  • Platforms that limit researchers' ability to develop novel methodologies
  • Systems that prioritize efficiency over creative exploration

docs.title: Insight Generation
docs.text:
• AI analysis tools that produce conventional interpretations rather than transformative insights
  • Reporting systems that follow formulaic templates without room for creative expression
  • Workflows that reduce opportunities to respond creatively to unexpected findings

docs.title: Preserving Creative Capacities
docs.text: Strategies to protect creative capacities in AI-augmented research: - Design tools that prompt researchers to generate alternative interpretations - Create 'sandbox' environments where researchers can experiment with novel approaches - Structure projects to include dedicated time for creative exploration - Develop training that emphasizes the value of creative risk-taking in research - Ensure AI adoption preserves opportunities to encounter and learn from failure

docs.title: Connection to Habituation Process
docs.text: Creative capacities develop through the habituation process: - 'Skill generally cannot be learnt through testimony, and requires practice' - Creative development involves 'refinement of the action through successive trials and learning from mistakes' - Encountering and overcoming disappointment and failure are essential components - Creative expertise develops through stages from novice to expert

docs.title: Contrast with Technical Skills
docs.text: Unlike technical skills that may become obsolete, creative capacities are fundamental to human flourishing. Their impoverishment leads to diminished lives, explaining why capacity-deskilling should always be a cause for worry. In market research, preserving creative capacities is essential for generating insights that go beyond what AI systems can produce, maintaining the competitive advantage of human researchers.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A neo-Aristotelian approach to human flourishing where flourishing is understood as a complex, unified, and well-rounded life, providing the philosophical foundation for understanding why capacity-deskilling is harmful. As detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, this framework explains why impoverished capacities lead to impoverished lives.

docs.title: Philosophical Foundation
docs.text:
Developmental Perfectionism, as articulated by Kauppinen (2025) and building on Hurka (1993), holds that: - Human flourishing is a complex, unified, and well-rounded life - Humans exercise capacities in activities that yield intrinsically valuable outcomes - The competent exercise of capacities is the manifestation of achieving intrinsically valuable goods - The value of an achievement comes from the competent exercise of capacities, not merely from the outcome

As Ferdman explains, 'the value of being on the summit of Mt. Everest is gained from the competent exercise of a combination of capacities involved in climbing it, and not from simply being there (say, if one arrives there by helicopter).'

docs.title: Core Human Capacities
docs.text: The framework identifies four core capacities that constitute human flourishing:

docs.title: Epistemic Capacities
docs.text:
• Theoretical rationality: thinking, considering reasons to believe, forming beliefs, contemplating
  • Practical rationality (phronesis/common sense or wisdom): doing the right thing in the right way for the right reason

docs.title: Social Capacities
docs.text:
• Moral capacity: recognizing others as moral agents, making ethical judgments
  • Relational capacity: forming meaningful relationships of friendship and love

docs.title: Creative Capacities
docs.text:
• Generating novel ideas
  • Making unfamiliar combinations of familiar concepts
  • Transforming conceptual spaces without relying on luck or mechanical procedures

docs.title: Volitional Capacity
docs.text:
• The ability to exert effort, overcome difficulty, persevere, and grow
  • Required to achieve intrinsically valuable goals
  • Functions as a meta-capacity necessary for developing all other capacities

docs.title: Why Capacity-Deskilling is Harmful
docs.text: Developmental Perfectionism explains why capacity-deskilling is problematic: - Impoverished capacities lead to impoverished lives - Inadequate development of capacities diminishes us as humans - Unlike skill obsolescence (e.g., hunting, basket-weaving), capacity deskilling should always be a cause for worry - Deskilling undermines our ability to achieve intrinsically valuable goods

docs.title: AI's Threat to Human Flourishing
docs.text: Ferdman applies this framework to show how AI systems threaten human flourishing by: - Creating capacity-hostile-environments that restrict opportunities for capacity development - Undermining the habituation process necessary for skill development - Reducing opportunities for embodiment in skilling through disembodied interaction - Encouraging plan-following rather than plan-forming, diminishing practical wisdom

docs.title: Market Research Implications
docs.text: This framework explains: - Why the entry-level squeeze is problematic - it eliminates opportunities for capacity development - The structural nature of the human-operating-model-gap - Why high-intensity AI adopters must intentionally design environments for capacity development - The limitations of technical upskilling without addressing capacity cultivation

docs.title: Societal Obligation
docs.text: Developmental Perfectionism implies a societal obligation to: - Foster capacity-conducive-environments that encourage embodied interaction - Design public goods that support the habituation process - Create conditions where individuals can develop and exercise all core capacities - Address the structural conditions that create capacity-hostile environments

docs.title: Contrast with Individual Responsibility
docs.text: Unlike approaches that expect individuals to 'be virtuous superheroes' and will themselves to cultivate capacities, Developmental Perfectionism: - Recognizes environmental constraints on capacity development - Identifies systemic conditions that create capacity-hostile environments - Calls for societal solutions rather than individual willpower - Focuses on designing environments conducive to human flourishing

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The essential role of physical presence and sensory experience in the development of human capacities, particularly social and moral skills. Embodied interaction is critical for recognizing others as moral agents and forming meaningful relationships, as analyzed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem.

docs.title: Philosophical Foundation
docs.text: Ferdman draws on the Enactive Approach in cognition to establish that: - Embodied 'participatory sense-making' is constitutive of social cognition - Social interaction itself and its emergent dynamics constitute an essential part of the cognitive process - Meaning is generated and transformed 'in the interplay between the unfolding interaction process and the individuals engaged in it' - Without embodied interaction, recognizing others as moral agents requires more mental effort

docs.title: Critical Role in Capacity Development
docs.text: Embodiment is essential for developing:

docs.title: Moral Capacities
docs.text:
• Perceiving others as embodied beings similar to ourselves through voice and gaze
  • Developing 'embodied understanding' of others as similar loci of embodied subjectivity
  • Spontaneous recognition of others as moral agents through embodied interaction

docs.title: Social Capacities
docs.text:
• Forming meaningful friendships that are diminished in disembodied environments
  • Creating shared experiences necessary for shared valuing of capacities
  • Developing relational skills through physical presence and nonverbal communication

docs.title: Epistemic Capacities
docs.text:
• Developing practical wisdom through real-world, embodied experience
  • Cultivating discernment through embodied assessment of situations
  • Building trust through embodied interaction that cannot be replicated digitally

docs.title: AI's Threat to Embodied Skilling
docs.text: Digital environments threaten embodied skilling by: - Creating 'disembodied interactions' that make it harder to form meaningful relationships - Requiring more discipline for a diminished experience of virtue friendships - Fracturing the user's affordance space into disconnected fields - Leading to alienation rather than offering opportunities for mutually informing skills

docs.title: Market Research Implications
docs.text: The shift to remote and AI-mediated research threatens capacity development through: - Reduced opportunities for embodied client interaction - Diminished development of social capacities necessary for relationship-based research - Weakened moral attention in research design and interpretation - Impoverished habituation process for junior researchers

docs.title: Preserving Embodied Skilling
docs.text: Strategies to maintain embodied interaction in AI-augmented research: - Design research workflows that preserve opportunities for face-to-face client interaction - Create hybrid research models that combine digital tools with embodied engagement - Structure team collaboration to include regular in-person interaction - Develop training that emphasizes the irreplaceable value of embodied research practices - Ensure AI tools enhance rather than replace embodied aspects of research

docs.title: Connection to Capacity-Hostile Environments
docs.text: Disembodied environments often constitute narrow-field-of-affordances that restrict opportunities for capacity development. As Ferdman explains, 'without being embodied in a social interaction—without the return of the gaze of the other—we would be hard-pressed to recognize them spontaneously as moral agents.'

docs.title: Contrast with Plan-Following
docs.text: Embodied skilling supports plan-forming (active creation of plans through self-deliberation) rather than plan-following (executing pre-determined plans). Physical presence enables researchers to adjust their approach based on real-time embodied interaction with clients and stakeholders, developing the agential control necessary for complex research challenges.

docs.title: Entry level squeeze
docs.text: The entry-level squeeze describes the growing pressure on traditional entry-level positions in knowledge work as AI capabilities automate foundational tasks that historically served as training grounds for developing professional expertise.

docs.title: Capacity Development Challenges for Entry-Level Workers
docs.text: While recent evidence shows entry-level headcount is growing among high-intensity AI adopters, the nature of entry-level work is changing in ways that may affect capacity development for junior professionals.

docs.title: Deskilling Risks in Entry-Level Roles
docs.text:
The ai-deskilling-structural-problem framework reveals several risks for entry-level workers:

  • Reduced habituation opportunities: When AI automates routine tasks, entry-level workers lose "the routine opportunities to practice their judgment and strengthen their cognitive musculature" (Lee et al. 2025)
  • Shallow skill development: Entry into professions may become more superficial without proper mentoring
  • Disembodied learning: Digital workflows may limit embodied interaction necessary for social capacity development
  • Affordance shrinkage: Systematic reduction in action possibilities for developing practical wisdom

docs.title: Structural Dimensions
docs.text:
These challenges are not merely individual responsibility issues but stem from structural conditions:

"We develop and exercise our epistemic, moral, social, and creative capacities in response to our social and material environment" (Ferdman 2026). When entry-level environments become [[capacity-hostile]], junior professionals may struggle to develop the "arts of personhood" required for long-term success.

docs.title: Evidence from Research
docs.text: Studies show that young people growing up with digital tools already struggle with "everyday but essential" skills like empathy, time management, speaking to others, problem-solving and critical thinking (Halliday 2025). AI tools like artificial-personal-assistants could potentially exacerbate this deskilling.

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
For market research organizations, these findings suggest:

  • Entry-level training programs must intentionally preserve opportunities for capacity development
  • Mentorship relationships are crucial for counteracting AI-mediated deskilling
  • Workflows should balance AI augmentation with human skill development
  • Organizations should design capacity-conducive environments for junior staff

The structural perspective emphasizes that "we cannot expect agents to be what Mitcham (2024) calls 'virtuous superheroes' and properly cultivate their human capacities if their social environment does not value the full maturation of these capacities."

See capacity-conducive-environments and habituation-process for related frameworks addressing these challenges.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The human capacities related to knowledge, reasoning, and understanding, including theoretical rationality and practical rationality (phronesis), which are essential for navigating truth and making informed decisions. As detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, these capacities are constitutive of human flourishing and can be undermined by AI systems.

docs.title: Theoretical Rationality
docs.text:
• Thinking, considering reasons to believe, forming beliefs, contemplating
  • The capacity to acquire and evaluate knowledge
  • Essential for developing accurate understanding of situations
  • Involves critical thinking, analytical reasoning, and evidence evaluation

docs.title: Practical Rationality (Phronesis)
docs.text:
• Common sense or wisdom: doing the right thing in the right way for the right reason
  • The capacity to apply theoretical knowledge to practical situations
  • Involves discernment: correct understanding of how the good and bad apply in particular circumstances
  • Requires accurate assessment of testimony from others
  • Necessary for critically reflecting on conceptions of a flourishing life

docs.title: Role in Planning and Decision-Making
docs.text: Epistemic capacities are essential for effective planning: - Self-deliberation on values and goals requires theoretical rationality - Coordinating one's goals and intentions with one's actions requires practical wisdom - A wise person 'knows the effective means to one's ends and possesses an accurate understanding of their situation and circumstances' - Practical wisdom is 'necessary for critically reflecting on one's conceptions of a flourishing life, in order to set appropriate goals and strive to accomplish them in the right way'

docs.title: AI's Threat to Epistemic Capacities
docs.text: Ferdman identifies how AI systems undermine epistemic capacities: - Erosion of critical thinking and analytical reasoning through over-reliance on AI - Diminished diagnostic reasoning and clinical judgment in professional contexts - Reduced retention of tacit knowledge as systems automate routine tasks - Declining ethical sensitivity and weakened moral judgment - 'Depriving the user of routine opportunities to practice their judgment and strengthen their cognitive musculature'

docs.title: Entry-Level Research Positions
docs.text:
• AI automation of data collection and basic analysis eliminates routine tasks that served as training grounds for epistemic capacity development
  • Junior researchers miss opportunities to develop practical wisdom through successive attempts and learning from mistakes
  • Reduced opportunities for self-deliberation on research quality and methodology

docs.title: AI-Powered Analysis Tools
docs.text:
• Systems that generate insights without requiring researchers to justify conclusions
  • Platforms that present AI-generated recommendations as definitive rather than prompts for deliberation
  • Tools that offload analytical reasoning to AI without scaffolding for capacity development

docs.title: Preserving Epistemic Capacities
docs.text: Strategies to protect epistemic capacities in AI-augmented research: - Design tools that require researchers to explain and justify AI-generated insights - Create 'red team' processes where alternative interpretations are deliberately sought - Structure projects to maintain human oversight of critical analytical decisions - Develop training that emphasizes the researcher's role in evaluating AI outputs - Ensure AI adoption preserves opportunities for self-deliberation on research quality

docs.title: Connection to Capacity Development
docs.text: Epistemic capacities are interdependent with other capacities: - Developing practical wisdom requires volitional capacity to overcome difficulty - Effective planning requires social capacities for coordination with others - Responding to unexpected events requires creative capacities - Moral attention in research design requires embodiment in skilling

docs.title: Contrast with Technical Skills
docs.text: Unlike technical skills that may become obsolete (e.g., specific programming languages), epistemic capacities are fundamental to human flourishing. Their impoverishment leads to diminished lives, explaining why capacity-deskilling should always be a cause for worry rather than a neutral technological development.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The gradual process of becoming skilled through practice, involving inculcation through continued attunement to demands of individual cases, with critical implications for AI's impact on skill development. As detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, skill development cannot be learned through testimony alone but requires practice, encountering and overcoming disappointment and failure.

docs.title: Gradual Development
docs.text: Habituation occurs through stages from novice to expert, where: - Early stages involve more rule-following - Later stages feature rapid, fluid, involved engagement - The process itself is one of growth rather than simple repetition - Competence develops through successive attempts at an activity

docs.title: Two Essential Components
docs.text:
1. Intersubjectivity: Skill habituation has a 'shared understanding' dimension requiring:
  2. Mentors to guide novices into becoming experts
  3. Shared valuing of both the skill and its outputs

  4. Social practices that generate moral reasons for action

  5. Embodiment: Successful habituation must include an embodied component where:

  6. 'Meaning is generated and transformed in the interplay between unfolding interaction and participants'
  7. Embodied interaction enables recognition of others as moral agents
  8. Physical presence creates opportunities for 'participatory sense-making'

docs.title: AI's Impact on Habituation
docs.text: Ferdman identifies how AI systems threaten the habituation process: - Automating routine tasks 'deprives the user of routine opportunities to practice their judgment and strengthen their cognitive musculature' - Creating environments where users respond to AI outputs as environmental triggers rather than initiating activities - Reducing embodied interaction necessary for moral and social capacity development - Offloading planning activities that would otherwise develop practical wisdom

docs.title: Examples in Market Research
docs.text: The entry-level squeeze occurs because AI automation eliminates the routine tasks that previously served as: - Habituation opportunities for junior researchers - Context for developing practical wisdom through real-world experience - Foundation for building client relationships through embodied interaction - Pathway to understanding research quality through successive attempts

docs.title: Preserving Habituation in AI Era
docs.text: Strategies to maintain effective habituation: - Design AI tools that require researchers to explain and justify AI-generated insights - Create 'scaffolded' workflows where junior researchers gradually assume responsibility - Ensure AI adoption doesn't eliminate the routine tasks necessary for skill development - Structure mentorship programs that explicitly cultivate shared valuing of research capacities - Maintain opportunities for embodied client interaction even when using AI tools

docs.title: Connection to Human Flourishing
docs.text: The habituation process is essential for developing the epistemic, social, creative, and volitional capacities that constitute human flourishing under the developmental-perfectionism framework. Without proper habituation, researchers risk capacity impoverishment that undermines their professional effectiveness and personal fulfillment.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Core abilities that constitute human flourishing, including epistemic, social, creative, and volitional capacities, which are fundamental to being human and can be undermined by AI systems. As detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, these capacities are constitutive of our flourishing, and their impoverishment leads to diminished lives.

docs.title: Epistemic Capacities
docs.text:
• Theoretical rationality: Thinking, considering reasons to believe, forming beliefs, contemplating
  • Practical rationality (phronesis): Doing the right thing in the right way for the right reason, including discernment and accurate understanding of situations
  • Essential for navigating truth, making informed decisions, and developing practical wisdom

docs.title: Social Capacities
docs.text:
• Moral capacity: Recognizing others as moral agents, making ethical judgments, understanding moral reasons for action
  • Relational capacity: Forming meaningful relationships of friendship and love, understanding others' perspectives
  • Critical for participating in communal life and developing shared valuing of capacities

docs.title: Creative Capacities
docs.text:
• Generating novel ideas and making unfamiliar combinations of familiar concepts
  • Transforming conceptual spaces without relying merely on luck or mechanical procedures
  • Enabling innovation, adaptation, and responding to unexpected events in planning

docs.title: Volitional Capacity
docs.text:
• The ability to exert effort, overcome difficulty, persevere, and grow
  • Required to achieve intrinsically valuable goals
  • Functions as a meta-capacity necessary for developing all other capacities
  • Essential for the habituation process of skill development

docs.title: Interdependence of Capacities
docs.text: These capacities rarely operate in isolation: - The capacity to know involves theoretical rationality, practical rationality, volitional capacity, and physical capacities - Planning one's life requires epistemic capacities (self-deliberation), social capacities (coordination with others), creative capacities (responding to surprises), and volitional capacity (perseverance) - Moral attention requires embodied interaction that engages multiple capacities simultaneously

docs.title: Capacity-Skill Framework
docs.text: Ferdman conceptualizes capacities as skills through: - Agential control: Having the ability to adjust execution of actions as performance unfolds - Habituation: Gradual development through practice, attunement to individual cases, and learning from mistakes - Intersubjectivity: Learning through relationships with mentors who share the value of the skill - Embodiment: Physical presence and sensory experience essential for social and moral capacity development

docs.title: AI's Threat to Human Capacities
docs.text: AI systems threaten capacities by creating capacity-hostile-environments that: - Automate routine tasks that are essential for habituation ('depriving users of routine opportunities to practice their judgment') - Encourage plan-following rather than plan-forming, diminishing practical wisdom development - Reduce embodied interaction necessary for moral attention and relationship formation - Replace human mentors with algorithmic guidance, undermining intersubjective skilling

docs.text: Understanding human capacities explains: - Why the entry-level squeeze is problematic - it eliminates opportunities for capacity development - The structural nature of the human-operating-model-gap - Why high-intensity AI adopters grow entry-level roles by 12.0% - they preserve capacity development opportunities - The limitations of technical upskilling without addressing capacity cultivation

docs.text: Strategies to protect capacities in AI-augmented research: - Design workflows that maintain human oversight of critical decision points - Create 'scaffolded' projects that gradually increase researcher responsibility - Ensure AI tools require researchers to explain and justify AI-generated insights - Structure mentorship programs that explicitly cultivate shared valuing of research capacities - Preserve opportunities for embodied client interaction even when using AI tools
