Impoverished capacities lead to impoverished lives, explaining why capacity-deskilling should always be a cause for worry, unlike skill obsolescence in specific domains like hunting or basket-weaving.

docs.title: Human operating model gap
docs.text: The human operating model gap refers to the growing disparity between the rapid advancement of AI capabilities and the slower adaptation of human systems, processes, and skills required to leverage AI effectively within organizations.

docs.title: Workforce Composition Changes with AI Adoption
docs.text: Recent evidence reveals how AI adoption is reshaping workforce composition across roles, highlighting the growing gap between rapidly advancing AI capabilities and slower human system adaptation.

docs.title: Role-Specific Employment Effects
docs.text:
The ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study provides detailed evidence of how AI adoption affects different job functions:

  • Broad-based growth: High-intensity adopters showed growth across multiple roles:
  • Sales headcount: +10.3%
  • Administrative headcount: +7.8%
  • Engineering headcount: +7.3%
  • Customer service headcount: +6.3%

  • Scientist headcount: +5.6%

  • Entry-level expansion: Entry-level headcount rose 12.0% among high-intensity adopters

  • Managerial shifts: Manager-plus share fell by 1.52 percentage points despite overall growth

docs.title: Structural Workforce Shifts
docs.text:
These findings reveal several important patterns:

  1. Non-binary impact: AI adoption doesn't simply eliminate jobs but reshapes workforce composition
  2. Intensity matters: Only high-intensity adopters (top tercile of AI spend) showed significant growth
  3. Gradual emergence: Gains followed a learning curve, emerging 6-12 months after adoption
  4. Sector concentration: Effects were strongest in the Information sector

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
For market research organizations, these workforce shifts suggest:

  • AI is currently augmenting rather than replacing human capabilities in information work
  • Strategic AI investment may support growth across multiple functions
  • Entry-level positions may expand as firms scale with AI assistance
  • Workforce planning must account for the gradual nature of AI integration

The study notes that "the earliest signs of growth emerge roughly 6-12 months after adoption, perhaps after firms establish best practices, integrate AI tools into workflows, and are subsequently able to make new investments and hire staff."

docs.title: Bridging the Gap
docs.text:
To address the human operating model gap, market research firms should:

  • Develop AI adoption strategies that align with workforce development
  • Create pathways for employees to develop AI-augmented capabilities
  • Recognize that successful integration requires time for habituation
  • Design capacity-conducive environments that preserve opportunities for skill development

See value-chain-shift and ai-professionalization for related frameworks analyzing AI's impact on organizational structures.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The shared understanding dimension of skill development, where learning occurs through relationships with others who guide and share the value of the skill. Becoming skilled typically requires a mentor to instill not only mechanical aspects but also the value of the skill, as detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem.

docs.title: Philosophical Foundation
docs.text:
Ferdman explains that skill habituation has an essential intersubjective component: - Becoming skilled typically requires a mentor to guide the novice into becoming an expert - Mentors instill not only mechanical aspects of the skill but, as importantly, the value of the skill - In the mentor-mentee relationship, both develop shared intentions and 'shared valuing' of the skill - Social practices performed by groups or whole societies provide a mentoring environment

As Alasdair MacIntyre noted, 'learning is carried out through the practices of the common life: becoming the kind of agent who is responsive to whatever it is that skillful action requires... has to be learned from teachers and exemplars who know how to communicate this kind of responsiveness to others through the habits of a common life.'

docs.title: Individual Level
docs.text:
• Mentor-mentee relationships where shared valuing of both the skill and its outputs develops
  • The mentor helps the novice view the value of the skill as their own through guided practice
  • Shared experiences create the context for developing competence through successive attempts

docs.title: Societal Level
docs.text:
• Social practices performed by groups or whole societies provide mentoring environments
  • The family, colleagues, and citizens collectively generate moral reasons for action
  • Social practices have a constitutive aim or telos that ultimately helps people fare well
  • Shared valuing of capacities develops through participation in these practices

docs.title: AI's Threat to Intersubjective Skilling
docs.text: Artificial Personal Assistants (APAs) and other AI tools threaten intersubjective skilling by: - Replacing human mentors with algorithmic guidance - Providing recommendations without shared understanding of value - Creating environments where users interact primarily with non-human agents - Undermining opportunities for shared experiences necessary for capacity development

docs.title: Market Research Implications
docs.text: The entry-level squeeze occurs partly because AI automation reduces opportunities for: - Mentorship relationships between senior and junior researchers - Shared valuing of research quality through embodied interaction - Development of practical wisdom through social practices - Transmission of tacit knowledge through apprenticeship

docs.title: Preserving Intersubjectivity
docs.text: Strategies to maintain intersubjective skilling in AI-augmented research: - Design workflows that preserve human mentorship even when using AI tools - Create structured opportunities for shared reflection on research quality - Ensure AI tools support rather than replace the transmission of tacit knowledge - Develop communities of practice where researchers share insights and develop shared understanding - Structure projects to maintain embodied interaction between researchers and clients

docs.title: Connection to Capacity Development
docs.text:
Intersubjectivity is essential for developing: - Social capacities through relationships with others - Epistemic capacities through shared understanding of truth - Practical wisdom through guidance from experienced practitioners - Volitional capacity through shared motivation and accountability

Without intersubjective skilling, researchers risk developing only shallow expertise that lacks the depth and adaptability required for complex market research challenges.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The challenge that different AI adoption measurement approaches yield dramatically different findings about AI's economic impact. As demonstrated by the contrast between exposure-based studies and spending-based research like the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study, methodological choices fundamentally shape conclusions about AI's labor market effects.

docs.title: Evidence of Heterogeneity
docs.text:
Study Type Primary Method Key Employment Finding Example Exposure-based Occupational AI exposure scores Negative impact on entry-level jobs Brynjolfsson et al. (2025) Spending-based Observed AI vendor payments Positive impact at high intensity Ramp-Revelio study Survey-based Executive adoption surveys Mixed or positive impacts Yotzov et al. (2026)

The Ramp-Revelio study documents this heterogeneity through direct comparison: - Exposure-based studies predict job losses in high-exposure occupations - Spending-based research shows job growth among high-intensity adopters - The discrepancy stems from methodological differences, not contradictory realities

docs.title: Root Causes
docs.text: Three fundamental methodological differences drive these divergent findings:

docs.title: 1. Adoption Measurement
docs.text:
• Exposure scores: Measure theoretical task feasibility ("could AI do this?")
  • Spending data: Measure actual adoption behavior ("is the firm paying for AI?")
  • Surveys: Capture self-reported usage ("do executives say they use AI?")

As the Ramp-Revelio study notes: "These estimates are closer to the Ramp–Revelio paid-adoption series than the firm-weighted BTOS benchmark, but they still measure a different object."

docs.title: 2. Intensity Dimension
docs.text:
• Exposure scores: Typically binary or quintile-based
  • Spending data: Reveals continuous intensity effects (PEPM metric)
  • Surveys: Often lack precise intensity measures

The Ramp-Revelio study found only high-intensity adopters showed significant employment growth (+10.2%), while low-intensity adopters showed no change.

docs.title: 3. Selection Bias Handling
docs.text:
• Exposure scores: Cannot distinguish adopters from non-adopters with identical workforce
  • Spending data: Enables direct comparison of adopters vs. later adopters
  • Surveys: Often lack pre-adoption data for comparison

The Ramp-Revelio study documents substantial pre-adoption differences that confound simple adopter vs. non-adopter comparisons.

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
This methodological heterogeneity creates critical challenges:

  • Conflicting guidance: Different studies recommend opposite actions based on methodology
  • Implementation uncertainty: Hard to predict AI impact without knowing intensity threshold
  • Evaluation complexity: Must select appropriate methodology for specific context
  • Vendor claims: AI providers may cite favorable methodology while ignoring others

docs.title: Strategic Response Framework
docs.text:
Market research organizations should adopt a methodologically sophisticated approach:

  1. Triangulate findings: Consider evidence from multiple methodological approaches
  2. Assess intensity: Focus on high-intensity implementation for meaningful impact
  3. Control for selection: Account for pre-existing differences when evaluating AI
  4. Contextualize results: Recognize sector-specific effects (e.g., concentrated in Information)

docs.title: Cross-References
docs.text: This concept explains the contradictory findings between the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study (showing 12.0% entry-level growth) and exposure-based studies predicting job losses. It represents the methodological foundation for understanding the ai-adoption-selection-bias problem and the value of the ai-adoption-methodological-innovation in spending-based measurement.

docs.title: Practical Guidance
docs.text:
For market research professionals, navigating methodological heterogeneity requires: - Never relying on a single study's methodology for decision-making - Understanding the measurement approach behind any AI impact claim - Recognizing that "AI adoption" has no single empirical rate (as shown in Ramp-Revelio Figure 1) - Focusing on high-intensity implementation thresholds rather than binary adoption

Without this methodological sophistication, organizations risk making decisions based on incomplete or misleading evidence about AI's true impact.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An environment that provides limited action possibilities, restricting opportunities for the development and exercise of human capacities, a key mechanism through which AI systems can create capacity-hostile environments as detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem.

docs.title: Philosophical Foundation
docs.text: Drawing on Gibson's ecological approach to perception, Ferdman explains that: - The environment is a 'world of affordances' formed by the relationship between agent and environment - Affordances are not mere opportunities but invitations that influence agent behavior - A narrow field of affordances restricts the invitations for valuable activities - Without sufficient invitations, the capacities involved in these activities will not be triggered

docs.title: Affordance Shrinkage
docs.text:
• Systematic, enduring, and deeply entrenched reduction in action possibilities
  • Discourages users from finding compensatory pathways due to cumulative effect
  • Creates environments where users respond to triggers rather than initiating activities

docs.title: Capacity Impoverishment
docs.text:
• Limits opportunities for developing agential control over capacities
  • Restricts the habituation process necessary for skill development
  • Diminishes opportunities for intersubjectivity in skilling
  • Undermines the development of practical wisdom through real-world experience

docs.title: AI-Induced Narrowing
docs.text: Ferdman identifies how AI systems create narrow fields of affordances:

docs.title: Automation of Routine Tasks
docs.text:
• 'Deprives the user of routine opportunities to practice their judgment and strengthen their cognitive musculature'
  • Leaves users 'atrophied and unprepared when exceptions do arise'
  • Reduces opportunities to develop capacities through successive attempts

docs.title: Disembodied Interaction
docs.text:
• Smartphones and digital interfaces 'fracture the user's affordance space into disconnected fields'
  • Creates environments that 'ultimately lead to alienation, rather than offering opportunities for mutually informing skills'
  • Makes it harder to form meaningful relationships and recognize others as moral agents

docs.title: Plan-Following Environments
docs.text:
• AI tools like personal assistants afford 'becoming a plan-follower rather than a plan-former'
  • Reduce opportunities for self-deliberation and settling/coordination functions of planning
  • Create contexts where users 'respond to the APA's recommendations' rather than initiating planning

docs.title: Entry-Level Research Positions
docs.text:
• AI automation of data collection and basic analysis eliminates routine tasks that served as training grounds
  • Creates narrow affordance fields for junior researchers to develop practical wisdom
  • Reduces opportunities for embodied client interaction necessary for relationship building

docs.title: AI-Powered Reporting Tools
docs.text:
• Systems that generate research reports with minimal human input
  • Restrict opportunities to develop writing and analytical skills through practice
  • Diminish the habituation process necessary for research excellence

docs.title: Expanding Affordance Fields
docs.text: Strategies to create richer affordance environments: - Design AI tools that require researchers to explain and justify AI-generated insights - Structure workflows to maintain human oversight of critical decision points - Create 'scaffolded' projects that gradually increase researcher responsibility - Ensure AI adoption preserves opportunities for embodied client interaction - Develop mentorship programs that explicitly cultivate shared valuing of research capacities

docs.title: Connection to Human Flourishing
docs.text: A narrow field of affordances undermines the neo-Aristotelian concept of developmental-perfectionism, where flourishing requires a complex, unified, and well-rounded life achieved through competent exercise of multiple capacities. Without sufficient action possibilities, researchers cannot develop the integrated capacities necessary for professional excellence and personal fulfillment.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: PEPM (AI Spend Per Employee) is a metric developed in the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study to measure the intensity of AI adoption at the firm level. It calculates monthly AI vendor spend per employee over the first three months after sustained AI adoption begins.

docs.title: Formula
docs.text:
PEPM = (Σ²ₘ₌₀ AIᵢ,ɢᵢ₊ₘ) / (3 × HCᵢ,ɢᵢ₋₁)

Where: - AIᵢ,ɢᵢ₊ₘ = AI vendor spend for firm i in month m after adoption - HCᵢ,ɢᵢ₋₁ = baseline headcount in the month before adoption

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
1. AI adoption is defined as the first month of a three-consecutive-month spell where AI spend is at least $100 monthly
  2. PEPM is calculated using AI spend over the first three months after adoption begins
  3. Baseline headcount is measured in the month before adoption
  4. Firms are sorted into intensity groups:
  5. High intensity: top PEPM tercile
  6. Low intensity: bottom two PEPM terciles

docs.title: Significance
docs.text:

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Plan-following refers to the execution of pre-determined plans without exercising agential control over the planning process itself. As analyzed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, this represents a habitual mode of action where individuals respond to environmental triggers rather than initiating and adjusting plans through self-deliberation.

docs.title: Habitual Nature
docs.text:
• Executing plans constructed by others rather than forming one's own
  • Responding to triggers in the environment rather than initiating activity
  • Lacking control over the 'settling' function (deciding between options)
  • Absence of the capacity to will oneself into initiating the planning activity

docs.title: Contrast with Plan-Forming
docs.text:
Plan-following differs fundamentally from plan-forming: - Plan-forming: Involves self-deliberation, agential control, and responsibility for outcomes - Plan-following: Involves responding to pre-determined recommendations without initiating the planning process

As Ferdman explains, 'forming a plan by self-deliberation requires exercising control over all the steps of the activity of forming the plan, including over initiating the two functions of planning: settling (deciding between options) and coordinating.' In contrast, 'relying on an APA to form our plans for us is more like a habit that is developed in response to a trigger in the environment.'

docs.title: AI's Role in Promoting Plan-Following
docs.text: Artificial Personal Assistants (APAs) and other AI tools encourage plan-following by: - Providing constant recommendations that users respond to as environmental triggers - Designing interfaces that 'prompt you to prioritize today's work' and 'schedule tasks logically' - Creating environments where users 'respond to the APA's recommendations' rather than initiating planning - Offering 'help me plan my day' and 'how should I fill an unscheduled hour' functionality that replaces self-deliberation

docs.title: Capacity Deskilling Effects
docs.text: Plan-following contributes to capacity deskilling by: - Reducing opportunities to develop practical wisdom through real-world experience - Diminishing the habituation process necessary for skill development - Undermining the development of agential control over capacities - Creating environments where users 'are not initiating the two functions of planning: settling and coordinating' - Reducing opportunities to take responsibility for outcomes and learn from mistakes

docs.title: AI-Powered Research Tools
docs.text:
• Systems that generate research questions and methodology without researcher input
  • Platforms that automate client reporting with minimal human oversight
  • Tools that offload analytical reasoning to AI without requiring researchers to justify conclusions

docs.title: Workflow Automation
docs.text:
• Scheduling tools that automatically assign research tasks
  • Project management systems that dictate research workflows
  • AI assistants that provide step-by-step guidance through research processes

docs.title: Structural Solutions
docs.text: To counteract plan-following tendencies in AI-augmented research: - Design tools that require researchers to explain and justify AI-generated insights - Structure workflows to maintain human oversight of critical planning decisions - Create 'red team' processes where alternative research approaches are deliberately sought - Ensure AI tools support rather than replace the researcher's role as ultimate decision-maker - Develop training that emphasizes the researcher's responsibility for planning and execution

docs.title: Connection to Capacity-Hostile Environments
docs.text: Plan-following is a key mechanism through which AI systems create capacity-hostile-environments: - It represents a narrow field of affordances that discourages users from seeking alternative pathways - It undermines the intersubjective habituation process necessary for capacity development - It reduces opportunities for embodied interaction in planning activities - It diminishes the volitional capacity required to initiate and adjust plans

docs.title: Contrast with Plan-Forming
docs.text: Unlike plan-forming environments that support capacity-conducive-environments, plan-following environments: - Restrict opportunities for developing practical wisdom - Diminish the habituation process through reduced practice - Create conditions where users become dependent on external guidance - Undermine the development of agential control over capacities

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The distinction between actively creating plans through self-deliberation (requiring agential control) versus executing pre-determined plans (more habitual), with critical implications for AI's impact on capacity development as analyzed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem.

docs.title: Philosophical Foundation
docs.text: Drawing on Bratman's theory of agency, Ferdman explains that: - Humans are 'essentially planning creatures,' and planning is a manifestation of practical rationality - Planning serves two agential functions: settling (managing finite cognitive resources) and coordination (imposing coherence constraints) - Planning facilitates coordination both over time and with other persons - Planning involves responding to unexpected events that can be sources of value and growth

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
• Involves self-deliberation on values and goals
  • Requires exercising agential control over initiating the planning activity
  • Includes both settling (deciding between options) and coordinating functions
  • Involves taking responsibility for outcomes to enable self-critique and improvement
  • Requires the full exercise of epistemic capacities, social capacities, and creative capacities

docs.title: Capacity Development
docs.text: Plan-forming supports capacity development by: - Providing opportunities to exercise practical wisdom in assessing situations - Creating contexts for developing discernment through real-world experience - Allowing for growth through responding to unexpected events - Requiring the volitional capacity to overcome difficulty and persevere

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
• Executing pre-determined plans constructed by others
  • Responding to triggers in the environment rather than initiating activity
  • Absence of the capacity to will oneself into initiating the planning activity
  • More habitual than skilled, as it lacks control over initiating the task

docs.title: Capacity Deskilling
docs.text: Plan-following contributes to capacity deskilling by: - Reducing opportunities to develop practical wisdom through real-world experience - Diminishing the habituation process necessary for skill development - Creating environments where users 'respond to the APA's recommendations' rather than initiating planning - Undermining the development of agential control over capacities

docs.title: AI's Impact on Planning
docs.text: Ferdman analyzes how AI tools like personal assistants threaten plan-forming: - APAs 'afford the replacement of many of the activities involved in both planning and executing one's plans' - Systems like Sunsama 'prompt you to prioritize today's work' and 'schedule tasks logically,' reducing user agency - Constant availability 'discourages the user from seeking out new opportunities for growth and exploration' - Long-term reliance limits 'agents' ability to transition to develop the capacities on their own'

docs.title: AI-Powered Research Tools
docs.text:
• Systems that generate research questions, methodology, and conclusions without researcher input
  • Platforms that automate client reporting with minimal human oversight
  • Tools that offload analytical reasoning to AI without requiring researchers to justify conclusions

docs.title: Structural Solutions
docs.text: To preserve plan-forming in AI-augmented research: - Design tools that require researchers to explain and justify AI-generated insights - Structure workflows to maintain human oversight of critical planning decisions - Create 'red team' processes where alternative research approaches are deliberately sought - Ensure AI tools support rather than replace the researcher's role as ultimate decision-maker - Develop training that emphasizes the researcher's responsibility for planning and execution

docs.title: Connection to Capacity Development
docs.text: The plan-forming vs plan-following distinction is central to understanding how AI affects capacity development: - Plan-forming environments support capacity-conducive-environments - Plan-following environments create capacity-hostile-environments - Preserving plan-forming opportunities is essential for addressing the human-operating-model-gap - Maintaining plan-forming capacity explains why high-intensity AI adopters grow entry-level roles by 12.0% - they preserve opportunities for junior researchers to develop through planning

docs.title: Seniorised roles
docs.text: The phenomenon where entry-level roles increasingly demand skills traditionally required in senior positions due to AI adoption.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: Seniorised roles describe the accelerating trend where entry-level positions now require skills traditionally associated with senior roles, driven by AI automation of foundational tasks. Figure 8 in the PwC 2026 report provides compelling evidence: in the US top AI exposure quartile, seniorised entry-level job postings are projected to grow 35% between 2019-2025, while non-seniorised roles decline by 10%. This occurs because AI tools handle routine onboarding tasks (e.g., data entry for [[inventory-clerks]] or basic analysis for [[recruiters]]), compressing career ladders and elevating entry requirements. Common senior skills now appearing in entry-level descriptions include strategic decision-making frameworks, cross-departmental collaboration, client advisory capabilities, and complex problem-solving—particularly in high-growth professionalised-jobs. Figure 7 contextualizes this within broader market trends, showing high AI exposure quartile entry-level postings have flatlined since 2022, suggesting seniorisation may be a prerequisite for growth in AI-impacted roles. The report warns this trend could exacerbate early-career inequality if not balanced with structured mentorship, as new graduates face higher barriers without prior exposure to advanced skills. However, organizations using the ai-job-future-framework can mitigate risks by designing onboarding that combines AI tools with human skill development. The phenomenon represents a key manifestation of AI's impact on career progression, with implications for education systems needing to prepare students for accelerated responsibility in the AI era.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The human capacities related to forming meaningful relationships, understanding others' perspectives, and participating in communal life, including moral capacity and relational capacity. As detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, these capacities are constitutive of human flourishing and can be undermined by AI systems.

docs.title: Moral Capacity
docs.text:
• Recognizing others as moral agents
  • Making ethical judgments and understanding moral reasons for action
  • Developing moral attention through embodied interaction
  • Understanding the constitutive aim or telos of social practices

docs.title: Relational Capacity
docs.text:
• Forming meaningful relationships of friendship and love
  • Understanding others' perspectives and building trust
  • Participating in communal life and shared valuing of capacities
  • Developing the ability to coordinate with others toward complex goals

docs.title: Role in Planning and Decision-Making
docs.text: Social capacities are essential for effective planning: - Planning involves coordinating with others toward achieving complex goals - Social relationships provide the context for understanding reasons for action - 'Our life goals (e.g., being a good parent, help combat climate change) are... drawn from our social relationships' - Shared experiences create the foundation for developing practical wisdom

docs.title: AI's Threat to Social Capacities
docs.text: Ferdman identifies how AI systems undermine social capacities: - Creating disembodied environments that make it 'harder to form meaningful friendship because technologically mediated virtue friendships require more discipline for a diminished experience' - Reducing opportunities for 'embodied understanding' of others as similar loci of subjectivity - Undermining the spontaneity of recognizing others as moral agents - Diminishing shared experiences necessary for shared valuing of capacities - 'AI mediation might come at the expense of human interaction, decreasing the opportunity to develop our capacities in concert with other humans'

docs.title: Client Relationships
docs.text:
• AI tools that replace face-to-face client interaction with chatbots
  • Platforms that automate client reporting without opportunities for embodied relationship building
  • Systems that reduce researchers' opportunities to develop trust with clients

docs.title: Team Collaboration
docs.text:
• Remote work tools that diminish embodied interaction among research teams
  • AI systems that replace human mentorship with algorithmic guidance
  • Workflows that reduce opportunities for shared reflection on research quality

docs.title: Preserving Social Capacities
docs.text: Strategies to protect social capacities in AI-augmented research: - Design research workflows that preserve opportunities for face-to-face client interaction - Create hybrid research models that combine digital tools with embodied engagement - Structure team collaboration to include regular in-person interaction - Develop mentorship programs that explicitly cultivate shared valuing of research capacities - Ensure AI tools enhance rather than replace the relational aspects of research

docs.title: Connection to Embodiment
docs.text: Social capacities depend critically on embodiment in skilling: - 'Without being embodied in a social interaction—without the return of the gaze of the other—we would be hard-pressed to recognize them spontaneously as moral agents' - Embodied interaction enables 'participatory sense-making' where meaning is generated through the interplay between participants - Physical presence creates opportunities for developing moral attention and relational skills

docs.title: Contrast with Technical Skills
docs.text: Unlike technical skills that may become obsolete, social capacities are fundamental to human flourishing. Their impoverishment leads to diminished lives, explaining why capacity-deskilling should always be a cause for worry. In market research, preserving social capacities is essential for maintaining the human element that distinguishes high-quality insights from automated data analysis.

docs.title: Superstar effect
docs.text: The top 20% of most AI-exposed companies, referred to as 'superstars', achieve a significantly higher productivity growth rate.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: The 'superstar effect' identifies a critical divergence among AI adopters: the top 20% of most AI-exposed firms achieve dramatically higher productivity gains than peers. This effect was documented by pwc using orbis company financial data. As revealed in Figure 12 of the PwC 2026 report, these 'superstar' companies attained 163% average productivity growth in 2025—5 times higher than the 33.5% growth rate of most AI-exposed companies as a whole. This advantage has widened steadily since 2022, with superstars accelerating their lead while other AI-exposed firms maintain moderate growth. Figure 13 shows this productivity advantage translates to headcount growth, with superstar firms expanding employment 52.2% by 2025 versus 35.7% for least exposed quartiles. Crucially, Figure 14 demonstrates these gains are shared with workers through higher wage growth (24.4% vs 16.6% in 2025). The report attributes superstar status to three factors: strategic AI integration beyond automation (leveraging the ai-job-future-framework), investment in complementary human skills, and organizational agility in addressing [[ai's limitations]]. This creates a 'winner-takes-most' dynamic where superstars capture disproportionate value—evident in Figure 16's AI specialist hiring surge within these firms. The effect has profound implications: companies failing to achieve superstar status risk falling behind in the AI transformation, while workers in superstar firms gain through both wages and career opportunities in high-growth professionalised-jobs. Policymakers must address resulting market concentration through targeted support for mid-tier AI adopters.

docs.title: Value chain shift
docs.text: The value chain shift refers to the fundamental repositioning of where value is created within market research and insights organizations as AI capabilities advance.

docs.title: Sectoral Variations in AI Impact
docs.text: Recent research reveals that AI's impact on the value chain is unevenly distributed across sectors, with significant implications for how value is created within market research organizations.

docs.title: Sectoral Employment Effects
docs.text:
The ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study found that employment gains from AI adoption are concentrated in the Information sector:

  • Information sector: 13.4% headcount growth among high-intensity AI adopters
  • Professional and technical services: Positive but non-significant growth
  • All other sectors: Near-zero or imprecise effects

This pattern reflects the current state of AI adoption, which is "uniquely concentrated in Information" where "the most commercially mature AI gains appear clearest in coding-agent and software-engineering workflows."

docs.title: Implications for Market Research Value Chain
docs.text:
For market research firms, this sectoral variation suggests:

  1. Front-end transformation: Research design and data collection may see earlier AI integration
  2. Back-end resilience: Interpretation and strategic recommendation may remain more human-intensive
  3. Specialization opportunities: Firms focusing on information-intensive research may adopt AI more rapidly
  4. Competitive differentiation: Early AI adopters in research may gain productivity advantages

The study notes that "it is still early in the AI adoption curve" and "AI use cases may diffuse more slowly outside software and media." This suggests market research firms should anticipate a gradual shift in where value is created, rather than an immediate transformation.

docs.title: Strategic Considerations
docs.text:
Market research organizations should consider:

  • Where their work aligns with sectors experiencing the strongest AI impacts
  • How to position themselves to benefit from productivity gains in information processing
  • When to invest in high-intensity AI adoption versus more limited applications
  • How to develop workforce strategies that align with sector-specific AI adoption patterns

See human-operating-model-gap and ai-professionalization for related frameworks analyzing AI's impact on organizational value chains.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The human capacity to exert effort, overcome difficulty, persevere, and grow in order to achieve intrinsically valuable goals, treated as a meta-capacity necessary for developing all other capacities. As detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, this capacity is essential for the habituation process of skill development and can be undermined by AI systems.

docs.title: Effort and Perseverance
docs.text:
• The ability to exert sustained effort toward challenging goals
  • Overcoming difficulty and persisting through obstacles
  • Maintaining focus and commitment despite setbacks
  • Growing through the process of striving toward valuable ends

docs.title: Meta-Capacity Function
docs.text:
• Required for developing and exercising all other human capacities
  • Enables the habituation process necessary for skill development
  • Supports the ability to initiate activities rather than merely responding to environmental triggers
  • Essential for taking responsibility for outcomes and learning from mistakes

docs.title: Role in Planning and Skill Development
docs.text: Volitional capacity is essential for effective planning and skill acquisition: - Required to 'resist the temptation to outsource the activity of planning to an external entity or tool' - Necessary for initiating the planning activity itself (the 'settling' function) - Enables researchers to 'develop and exercise the aforementioned capacities' - Critical for the habituation process: 'skill generally cannot be learnt through testimony, and requires practice'

docs.title: AI's Threat to Volitional Capacity
docs.text: Ferdman identifies how AI systems undermine volitional capacity: - Providing constant assistance that 'discourages the user from seeking out new opportunities for growth and exploration' - Creating environments where users 'respond to the APA's recommendations' rather than initiating activities - Offloading planning activities that would otherwise develop perseverance and effort - Reducing opportunities to encounter and overcome disappointment and failure - 'Long-term reliance on the APAs as a life coach/personal assistant would be problematic... as its convenience and constant availability may limit agents' ability to transition to develop the capacities on their own'

docs.title: Entry-Level Development
docs.text:
• AI automation of routine tasks eliminates opportunities for junior researchers to develop perseverance through successive attempts
  • Reduced need to overcome research challenges diminishes opportunities to build volitional capacity
  • Systems that provide instant answers reduce the need for sustained effort in problem-solving

docs.title: Research Excellence
docs.text:
• Diminished volitional capacity leads to reduced ability to tackle complex, ambiguous research problems
  • Over-reliance on AI tools reduces opportunities to develop the perseverance necessary for breakthrough insights
  • Convenience of AI-generated reports diminishes motivation to pursue deeper understanding

docs.title: Preserving Volitional Capacity
docs.text: Strategies to protect volitional capacity in AI-augmented research: - Design workflows that require researchers to persist through challenging problems - Create 'productive struggle' opportunities where AI tools don't provide immediate answers - Structure projects to include meaningful challenges that require sustained effort - Develop training that emphasizes the value of perseverance in research excellence - Ensure AI adoption preserves opportunities to encounter and learn from failure

docs.title: Connection to Capacity Development
docs.text: Volitional capacity is foundational to all other capacities: - Required for the habituation process of skill development - Necessary for exercising agential control over capacities - Essential for developing practical wisdom through real-world experience - Supports the ability to engage in plan-forming rather than plan-following

docs.title: Contrast with Technical Skills
docs.text: Unlike technical skills that may become obsolete, volitional capacity is fundamental to human flourishing. Its impoverishment leads to diminished lives, explaining why capacity-deskilling should always be a cause for worry. In market research, preserving volitional capacity is essential for maintaining the drive and perseverance necessary for high-quality, insightful research that goes beyond what AI systems can produce.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Academic journal published by Springer focusing on the social, ethical, and philosophical implications of artificial intelligence and digital technologies, where ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem was published. Provides a venue for critical reflection on AI's societal impacts.

docs.title: Publication Details
docs.text:
• Publisher: Springer
  • Scope: Interdisciplinary research on AI's social, ethical, and philosophical dimensions
  • Relevance: Publishes theoretical and empirical work examining how AI systems affect human capacities, social structures, and ethical frameworks
  • Key Contribution: Provides a platform for structural analyses of AI's impact beyond individual responsibility frameworks

docs.title: Ferdman Paper Context
docs.text: The 2026 Ferdman paper 'AI deskilling is a structural problem' (AI & Society, 41, 3001–3013) represents a significant contribution to the journal's mission by: - Moving beyond individual responsibility frameworks to analyze systemic conditions - Introducing the concepts of 'capacity-hostile environments' and 'capacity-conducive environments' - Providing a philosophical framework for understanding AI's impact on human capacities - Analyzing how AI mediation affects the habituation process necessary for skill development

docs.title: Journal's Role in Skills Gap Research
docs.text: AI & Society contributes to market research skills gap analysis by: - Publishing theoretical work that explains why the entry-level squeeze occurs - Providing frameworks for understanding the human-operating-model-gap as a structural issue - Offering critical perspectives on how AI adoption affects capacity development - Highlighting the distinction between skill obsolescence and capacity deskilling

docs.title: Connection to Market Research Practice
docs.text: The journal's theoretical contributions have practical implications: - Explains why high-intensity AI adopters must intentionally design capacity-conducive environments - Provides the foundation for understanding how AI tools can undermine epistemic capacities in research - Offers frameworks for evaluating whether AI systems create narrow fields of affordances - Helps distinguish between productive automation and capacity-hostile AI implementation

docs.title: Critical Perspective
docs.text: Unlike industry reports that focus on technical skills gaps, AI & Society emphasizes: - The structural dimensions of AI's impact on human capacities - The philosophical foundations of human flourishing in the AI age - The societal obligation to foster environments conducive to capacity development - The limitations of individual responsibility frameworks for addressing deskilling

docs.title: Relevance to Research Firms
docs.text: Market research organizations should engage with AI & Society to: - Understand the theoretical foundations of capacity development - Design research workflows that preserve opportunities for skill habituation - Evaluate whether their AI tools create capacity-conducive or capacity-hostile environments - Develop strategies for maintaining the human capacities essential to quality research

docs.text: AI systems based on Large Language Models designed to assist with personal organization, life planning, and decision-making, with critical implications for capacity development as analyzed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. These tools can create capacity-hostile environments when they encourage users to become plan-followers rather than plan-formers.

docs.title: Current Implementations
docs.text:
• ChatGPT, Claude.ai, and Gemini used as personal assistants
  • Sunsama: Scheduling app that 'displays tasks synced from various software, alongside your calendar and unfinished tasks... prompts you to prioritize today's work... schedules tasks logically into your next available time slot'
  • Other productivity tools that integrate LLMs for life organization and planning

docs.title: Key Functions
docs.text:
• Organizing daily schedules and routines
  • Providing life-planning advice and goal setting
  • Offering social validation and self-regulation support
  • Giving interpersonal guidance and relationship advice
  • Helping users 'find purpose' and determine values
  • Providing 'an always-on sounding board with whatever subject-matter expertise you need'

docs.title: Capacity Deskilling Risks
docs.text: Ferdman identifies significant risks when APAs become over-relied upon:

docs.title: Plan-Following Environments
docs.text:
• Creating contexts where users 'respond to the APA's recommendations' rather than initiating planning
  • Reducing opportunities for self-deliberation on values and goals
  • Undermining the 'settling' function of planning (deciding between options)
  • Diminishing practical wisdom development through reduced real-world experience

docs.title: Habituation Process Disruption
docs.text:
• 'Depriving the user of routine opportunities to practice their judgment and strengthen their cognitive musculature'
  • Reducing the need to encounter and overcome disappointment and failure
  • Creating environments where users 'are not initiating the two functions of planning: settling and coordinating'

docs.title: Intersubjective Skilling Reduction
docs.text:
• Replacing human mentors with algorithmic guidance
  • Diminishing opportunities for shared experiences necessary for capacity development
  • Undermining the transmission of tacit knowledge through apprenticeship

docs.title: Research Workflow Tools
docs.text:
• AI assistants that automate research planning and methodology selection
  • Systems that generate research questions without researcher input
  • Platforms that dictate research workflows through algorithmic recommendations

docs.title: Structural Solutions
docs.text: To mitigate capacity deskilling risks in research contexts: - Design APA-like tools that require researchers to explain and justify AI-generated insights - Create 'scaffolded' assistance that gradually reduces support as researcher competence grows - Ensure AI tools maintain human oversight of critical planning decisions - Structure workflows to preserve opportunities for researcher-initiated planning - Develop training that emphasizes the researcher's role as ultimate decision-maker

docs.title: Contrast with Productive Automation
docs.text: Unlike automation that frees agents from drudgery (e.g., washing machines), APAs risk creating capacity-hostile environments because: - They replace activities central to human capacity development - They automate multiple spheres of human activity simultaneously - They discourage users from seeking alternative pathways for capacity exercise - Their cumulative effect creates systematic affordance shrinkage

docs.title: Connection to Capacity Development
docs.text: APAs highlight the tension between convenience and capacity development: - Their constant availability 'discourages the user from seeking out new opportunities for growth and exploration' - Long-term reliance 'may limit agents' ability to transition to develop the capacities on their own' - Unlike human mentors, APAs 'would not know to remove itself as the training wheels'

docs.title: Design Principles for Capacity-Conducive APAs
docs.text: To create AI assistants that support rather than undermine capacity development: - Prioritize plan-forming over plan-following by requiring user input at critical decision points - Provide scaffolding that gradually reduces support as user competence grows - Create opportunities for embodied interaction alongside digital assistance - Design interfaces that encourage self-reflection rather than passive acceptance of recommendations - Build in mechanisms for users to take responsibility for outcomes and learn from mistakes

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The Callaway-Sant'Anna framework is an econometric approach for analyzing treatment effects when units receive treatment at different times, as implemented in the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study to analyze the impact of AI adoption on employment.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
• Developed by Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021) to address limitations of conventional two-way fixed effects event studies
  • Designed for staggered adoption designs where firms begin treatment (AI adoption) at different points in time
  • Estimates group-time average treatment effects separately for different adoption cohorts
  • Compares earlier adopters to later adopters in the same intensity group while the later adopters have not yet adopted

docs.title: Implementation in Ramp-Revelio Study
docs.text:
• Used to estimate the relationship between firm-level AI adoption and employment
  • Applied separately to low and high AI intensity adoption groups
  • For high-intensity adopters, compared firms that adopted early to firms that would eventually be high-intensity adopters but hadn't yet adopted
  • Included NAICS sector fixed effects to address selection into early AI adoption

docs.title: Advantages Over Traditional Methods
docs.text:
• Better suited to heterogeneous treatment timing than single two-way fixed effects event studies
  • Reduces bias that can occur when treatment effects are heterogeneous across adoption cohorts
  • Allows for more precise estimation of dynamic treatment effects
  • Provides cleaner pre-treatment diagnostics for parallel trends assumption

docs.title: Key Findings Enabled by This Framework
docs.text:
• Revealed that high-intensity AI adopters grew employment by 10.2% following adoption
  • Showed that these gains emerged gradually over 18-24 months
  • Demonstrated that low-intensity adopters showed no statistically significant change in employment
  • Provided evidence against predictions that AI adoption would lead to broad job losses

docs.title: Lightcast
docs.text: Lightcast (formerly Emsi Burning Glass) is a labor market analytics company that provides detailed data on job postings, skills demand, and workforce trends. The company aggregates and analyzes millions of job postings from across the internet to create comprehensive labor market intelligence.

docs.title: Role in AI Research
docs.text: Lightcast data serves as a primary source for PwC's Global AI Jobs Barometer analysis. According to the 2026 report, the analysis examined over one billion online job advertisements across six continents, with Lightcast providing the underlying job posting data.

docs.title: Data Collection Methodology
docs.text:
Lightcast gathers job posting data through:

  • Web scraping of major job boards and company career sites
  • Partnerships with job posting aggregators
  • Direct feeds from some large employers
  • Historical archives dating back to 2012 for certain markets

The company processes this raw data to extract structured information about required skills, qualifications, compensation, and other job characteristics.

docs.title: Application in PwC's Research
docs.text:
In the PwC 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer, Lightcast data was used to:

  • Track changes in job posting volumes across different AI exposure levels
  • Analyze skill requirements and how they evolve over time
  • Calculate wage premiums for AI-related skills
  • Identify trends in entry-level hiring patterns
  • Measure growth in AI specialist positions

docs.title: Key Insights Enabled by Lightcast Data
docs.text:
Analysis of Lightcast data revealed several critical patterns:

  • AI specialist job postings grew eight times faster than total job postings from 2012-2025
  • Entry-level job postings in the highest AI exposure quartile flatlined after 2022
  • Skills needed for the most AI-exposed jobs are changing 2.2x faster than for the least exposed jobs
  • Wage premiums for AI skills reached 62% across all sectors in 2025

docs.title: Limitations and Considerations
docs.text:
While valuable, Lightcast data has certain limitations:

  • Primarily captures formal, online job postings (may miss informal hiring)
  • Coverage varies by country and time period
  • Skill extraction relies on natural language processing of job descriptions
  • May not fully capture internal mobility or promotions

Researchers using Lightcast data, like PwC, typically note these limitations and adjust their methodologies accordingly.

See also: pwc-2026-global-ai-jobs-barometer, pwc-ai-occupational-exposure-index

docs.title: ORBIS
docs.text: ORBIS is a comprehensive global business information database maintained by Bureau van Dijk (a Moody's Analytics company). It provides detailed financial, ownership, and operational data on millions of companies worldwide, serving as a critical resource for business intelligence and economic research.

docs.title: Role in AI Research
docs.text: In PwC's 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer, ORBIS data served as the primary source for company-level analysis, particularly regarding productivity, headcount, and wage growth metrics across different levels of AI exposure.

docs.title: Data Coverage
docs.text:
ORBIS includes information on:

  • Over 400 million companies globally
  • Financial statements and performance metrics
  • Ownership structures and corporate hierarchies
  • Industry classifications using standard systems like NAICS
  • Employment data and executive information

For the PwC analysis, the database provided longitudinal data from 2018-2025 for companies with consistent reporting.

docs.title: Application in PwC's Research
docs.text:
PwC used ORBIS data to:

  • Measure productivity growth (revenue per employee) across AI exposure levels
  • Track headcount changes at companies in different AI exposure quartiles
  • Analyze wage growth patterns relative to AI adoption
  • Identify the "superstar effect" among highly AI-exposed companies

docs.title: Key Insights Enabled by ORBIS Data
docs.text:
Analysis of ORBIS data revealed several critical patterns:

  • The most AI-exposed companies showed 33.5% productivity growth (2018-2025) compared to 18.7% for least exposed
  • Headcount growth at most AI-exposed companies reached 52.2% versus 23.3% for least exposed
  • Wage growth at most AI-exposed companies reached 24.4% versus 5.6% for least exposed
  • The top 20% of most AI-exposed companies ("superstars") achieved 163% productivity growth

docs.title: Methodological Considerations
docs.text:
PwC's analysis using ORBIS data included several important methodological notes:

  • Focus on larger formal firms with annual turnover of at least $50m USD
  • Exclusion of companies that exited the market during the period (creating survivorship bias)
  • Potential bias toward larger, more formalized companies in some countries
  • Company AI exposure determined by NAICS sector classification

These considerations mean the analysis reflects patterns among established businesses rather than the entire economy, but still provides valuable insights into how AI adoption correlates with business performance.

See also: pwc-2026-global-ai-jobs-barometer, superstar-effect

docs.title: PwC
docs.text: PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) is a multinational professional services network and one of the Big Four accounting firms. It provides audit and assurance, tax, and advisory services to corporations, governments, and non-profit organizations globally. With operations in 157 countries and over 360,000 employees, PwC serves as a leading authority on economic and labor market trends.

docs.title: Relevance to AI and Market Research
docs.text: PwC has emerged as a pivotal publisher of research on artificial intelligence's impact on the global labor market. Its annual Global AI Jobs Barometer report analyzes trends using data from over one billion job advertisements, providing critical insights for the market research industry. The firm's proprietary pwc-ai-occupational-exposure-index methodology has become a standard for measuring AI's workforce impact.

docs.title: Key Contributions
docs.text:
• Developed the epoch-score framework for measuring human capability reliance in occupations
  • Identified the dual trends of ai-democratization (52% of jobs) and ai-professionalization (22% of jobs)
  • Documented the superstar-effect where top AI-adopting companies achieve disproportionate productivity gains
  • Quantified wage premiums for ai-skills across economic sectors

PwC's research directly informs talent strategy for market research firms navigating AI adoption. Their data provides empirical validation for skills gap analyses and workforce planning.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Ramp is a financial operations platform that processes corporate card and bill pay transactions. It provides the AI Index for measuring AI adoption intensity through corporate spending data.

docs.title: Role in AI Research
docs.text: Ramp's data was central to the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study, which linked Ramp's line-item spending data with Revelio Labs' workforce records to study AI's impact on employment.

docs.title: AI Index Methodology
docs.text:
• Identifies AI spend from line items using vendor and line-item classification
  • Captures spending on foundational large language models, GPU cloud, model serving and inference, coding agents, API tokens, AI image and video generators, and AI search and research software
  • Defines AI adoption as the first month of a three-consecutive-month spell where AI spend is at least $100 monthly
  • Measures adoption intensity as monthly AI spend per employee (PEPM) over first three months after adoption

docs.title: Data Collection
docs.text:
• Observes cleared spend at the line-item level, including date, amount, merchant, firm identifiers, and line-item detail
  • Aggregates records to the firm-month level
  • Requires firms to have at least six consecutive months of total Ramp spend of $5,000+ to qualify for analysis

docs.title: Significance
docs.text: Ramp's data provides a direct measure of AI adoption through actual spending, overcoming limitations of occupational exposure scores and surveys. This revealed-adoption measure captures firms making sustained, organization-level AI purchases rather than one-off employee experiments.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Revelio Labs is a workforce intelligence platform that aggregates data from online professional profiles to construct longitudinal employment histories. It provides seniority classification and workforce composition data.

docs.title: Role in AI Research
docs.text: Revelio Labs' workforce data was central to the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study, which linked Revelio's employment records with Ramp's AI spending data to study AI's impact on employment.

docs.title: Data Collection Methodology
docs.text:
• Aggregates information from millions of publicly available online professional profiles
  • Constructs longitudinal employment histories for individual workers
  • Each profile contains information on employers, job titles, employment dates, locations, and other career characteristics
  • Uses a seven-point seniority field to define:
  • Entry-level headcount: seniority 1-2
  • Non-entry headcount: seniority 3-7
  • Manager-plus headcount: seniority 4-7
  • Applies weighting methodology to adjust for differential platform usage and improve representativeness

docs.title: Data Validation
docs.text:
• Prior validation exercises show weighted Revelio measures closely track benchmark labor market statistics
  • Similar worker-level employment histories have been used extensively in academic research

docs.title: Significance
docs.text: Revelio Labs provides granular workforce data that enables analysis of not just total firm employment but also hiring, attrition, occupational composition, worker seniority, and other workforce characteristics difficult to observe in traditional data sources.

docs.title: AI Spend Per Employee Methodology
docs.text: First Observed: 2026-07-03 Last Updated: 2026-07-03

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A direct measurement approach for quantifying firm-level AI adoption intensity by calculating monthly AI vendor spend per employee over the first three months after adoption begins. Developed by Ramp economists for the 2026 AI Jobs Impact Study, this methodology addresses limitations of occupational exposure scores and survey-based adoption measures.

docs.title: Calculation
docs.text:
PEPM_i = (Σ from m=0 to 2 of AI_{i,G_i+m}) / (3 × HC_{i,G_i-1})

Where: - AI_{it} = monthly AI vendor spend - G_i = first month of sustained AI adoption - HC_{i,G_i-1} = baseline headcount in month before adoption

docs.title: Implementation Steps
docs.text:
1. Adoption Definition: First month of earliest three-consecutive-month spell with ≥$100 AI spend monthly
  2. Intensity Measurement: Calculate PEPM using first three post-adoption months
  3. Group Classification: Low intensity = bottom two PEPM terciles, High intensity = top tercile
  4. Comparison Design: Compare earlier adopters to later adopters in same intensity group

docs.title: Advantages Over Alternative Methods
docs.text: Method Limitations PEPM Advantages Occupational exposure scores Vary only across occupations, not firms Measures actual firm adoption decisions Executive surveys Capture awareness not implementation Tracks payment data showing actual usage AI-related job postings Proxy for interest not adoption Measures direct financial commitment Resume AI skills Lagging indicator of adoption Captures immediate spending behavior

  • First three months of spending strongly predicts long-term adoption patterns

docs.title: Epoch score
docs.text: The EPOCH score measures the reliance on human capabilities in various occupations.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: The EPOCH score, pwc's proprietary metric, quantifies occupational reliance on human capabilities difficult for AI to replicate. Ranging 0-1, it evaluates dimensions including empathy, creativity, physical dexterity, and face-to-face interaction through job description analysis and expert assessment. Figure 10 of the 2026 report provides definitive validation: new tasks added to AI-exposed roles since 2022 show EPOCH scores 2.5 times higher in the top exposure quartile (0.47) versus bottom quartile (0.19), proving AI shifts work toward human-intensive activities. Figure 11 further demonstrates its significance by showing democratised roles (0.48) and professionalised roles (0.45) maintain substantially higher scores than low exposure roles (0.26), indicating both AI impact pathways increase human reliance. The methodology explains key economic trends: occupations with higher EPOCH scores in AI-exposed roles command greater wage premiums (Figure 15), as human skills become scarcer value drivers. Crucially, the score helps operationalize the ai-job-future-framework's 'AI's limitations' dimension by identifying tasks requiring human oversight. The report shows EPOCH scores are rising fastest in high-exposure roles (Figure 9), with the top quartile's score increasing 116% from 2023-2025. This metric has become essential for organizations mapping future skill requirements, particularly in designing professionalised-jobs and addressing the human elements of 'superstar' company success (Figure 12). Policymakers also use it to target workforce development initiatives where human capabilities provide sustainable competitive advantages.

docs.title: Pwc ai occupational exposure index
docs.text: PwC's proprietary methodology to measure the degree to which different occupations are exposed to AI capabilities.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: PwC's AI Occupational Exposure Index quantifies occupational susceptibility to AI through a multi-dimensional methodology. Ranging 0-1, it analyzes 2,000+ work activities across 800+ occupations, assessing technical feasibility, economic viability, and adoption timelines for AI automation. The 2026 report reveals 74% of jobs have meaningful exposure (quartiles 2-4), with the top quartile experiencing transformative impacts. Figure 3 demonstrates how the index interacts with expertise requirements, showing high-exposure jobs either increase (professionalisation) or decrease (democratization) expertise demands. The methodology underpins critical findings: Figure 7 uses it to segment entry-level job trends, Figure 9 to analyze skill change velocity (top quartile changing 2.2x faster), and Figure 12 to correlate exposure with productivity. Notably, the index evolved to incorporate generative AI capabilities post-2022, explaining accelerated impacts observed after ChatGPT's release. Organizations apply it to identify at-risk roles, prioritize reskilling, and benchmark against industry peers—particularly valuable for navigating the 'superstar effect' where top-quartile firms achieve 163% productivity growth. The report details sector-specific adaptations (e.g., healthcare's focus on diagnostic support roles), making it versatile for workforce planning. When combined with the epoch-score, the index forms the empirical foundation of the ai-job-future-framework, enabling organizations to systematically address all four framework questions. Its longitudinal design (2012-2025 data) provides unprecedented insight into AI's accelerating labor market transformation.

docs.title: Ai specialist roles
docs.text: Job roles specifically focused on the development, implementation, and maintenance of AI systems, growing eight times faster than total job postings.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: AI specialist roles are experiencing explosive growth, expanding eight times faster than total job postings according to Figure 16 of the PwC 2026 report. From a 2012 baseline of zero, these roles reached 11.0x growth by 2025 versus 2.0x for total postings, with acceleration intensifying post-2022. Figure 16b shows pervasive sector adoption: Technology, Media and Telecoms leads at 11.4% of sector roles, followed by Health Industries (4.0%), Financial Services (3.0%), and Manufacturing (2.0%). Core responsibilities include AI system architecture, prompt engineering, ethical governance, and domain-specific integration—often blending technical and business skills. Figure 15 confirms these roles command significant wage premiums averaging 62%, with Consumer Markets reaching 118%. The report identifies three growth drivers: urgent demand for AI implementation expertise, the need to address [[ai's limitations]] in quality control and edge cases, and regulatory compliance requirements. Crucially, Figure 12 links this growth to the 'superstar effect', as top-performing AI-exposed companies achieve 163% productivity growth by strategically deploying these specialists. Unlike traditional tech roles, modern AI specialists increasingly operate in hybrid functions (e.g., AI-augmented [[pharmacists]] or [[financial-analysts]]), requiring both domain knowledge and technical proficiency. This trend positions AI specialization as a critical career pathway across the economy, with implications for education systems needing to develop curricula aligned with the ai-job-future-framework.

docs.title: Democratised jobs
docs.text: Democratised jobs are occupations reshaped by AI to demand less human expertise, representing 52% of advertised positions globally.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: Democratised jobs—where AI automates more expert tasks, leaving less expert tasks for humans—constitute 52% of global postings but show distinct market patterns. Figure 2 illustrates this through roles like [[inventory-clerks]] (AI automates inventory management but humans move stock) and [[recruiters]] (AI screens CVs but humans negotiate contracts). While numerous, Figure 4 shows they've added skills at half the pace of professionalised roles (33% vs 68% growth 2018-2025), and Figure 5 confirms slower salary growth (26% vs 37% since 2021). However, Figure 11 reveals a critical nuance: democratised roles maintain the highest average epoch-score (0.48), indicating continued reliance on human capabilities for remaining tasks—often involving physical dexterity, adaptability in unstructured environments, or interpersonal interactions. This explains why these roles remain resilient despite reduced expertise requirements. The report warns that while democratisation expands job accessibility (e.g., enabling non-experts to perform complex analysis via AI tools), it may compress career ladders without structured progression paths. Figure 9 contextualizes this within skills transformation, showing democratised roles still experience 2.2x faster skill changes than low-exposure jobs. Organizations can leverage this trend through the ai-job-future-framework's 'Environmental forces' dimension, designing roles that combine AI efficiency with uniquely human execution—particularly valuable in sectors like retail and logistics where physical interaction remains essential.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Entry-level job postings in quartiles with lower AI exposure continue to grow, while those in the highest AI exposure quartile have flatlined since 2022. As documented in multiple studies, these positions represent critical training grounds for developing professional expertise through the habituation process.

docs.title: Contradictory Evidence
docs.text:
Recent research presents seemingly contradictory findings about entry-level job trends:

  • Exposure-based studies: Predict decline in entry-level roles due to AI automation
  • Spending-based research: Shows growth in entry-level roles among high-intensity AI adopters

The ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study resolves this contradiction by revealing: - High-intensity adopters (top PEPM tercile) grew entry-level headcount by 12.0% - Low-intensity adopters showed no statistically significant change - Gains emerged gradually, reaching significance around 6-12 months post-adoption - Growth was broad across functions: engineering, sales, admin, customer service

This explains why the entry-level-squeeze concept remains relevant despite overall growth—entry-level roles are growing only among firms making substantial AI investments.

docs.title: Structural Tensions
docs.text:
Entry-level positions face three competing forces:

  1. Automation pressure: AI systems can perform foundational tasks that traditionally served as training grounds
  2. Capacity development need: Junior staff require opportunities to develop through the habituation process
  3. Strategic value: High-intensity AI adopters recognize entry-level roles as essential for scaling AI-enhanced operations

This creates a bifurcated market where entry-level opportunities are shrinking in low-AI firms but expanding in high-AI firms.

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
The industry faces a critical challenge:

  • Traditional pathways: Junior researchers developing through manual analysis are becoming rare
  • New requirements: Entry-level roles increasingly demand human-intensive-skills alongside AI literacy
  • Capacity risk: Over-automation threatens the embodiment-in-skilling and intersubjectivity-in-skilling needed for deep expertise

The ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem study warns that without careful design, AI tools may create capacity-hostile environments where junior researchers miss critical development opportunities.

docs.title: Strategic Framework for Organizations
docs.text: Market research firms should adopt a dual approach:

docs.title: For High-Intensity AI Adopters
docs.text:
• Preserve foundational tasks: Create 'capacity zones' where junior staff develop without AI assistance
  • Structured progression: Gradually increase AI tool complexity as researchers develop
  • Mentorship integration: Pair AI tools with human guidance to maintain intersubjectivity-in-skilling

docs.title: For All Organizations
docs.text:
• Measure capacity development: Track skill progression alongside productivity metrics
  • Design capacity-conducive workflows: Ensure AI tools extend rather than replace the learning journey
  • Value human-intensive-skills: Recognize that AI augmentation increases demand for uniquely human capacities

docs.title: Cross-References
docs.text: This analysis synthesizes findings from the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study (showing 12.0% entry-level growth at high-intensity adopters) and ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem (warning about capacity erosion risks). It explains how the entry-level-squeeze operates within a context of overall growth among high-AI firms, creating a bifurcated job market.

docs.title: Practical Guidance

docs.title: AI Deskilling and Core Human Capacities
docs.text: Recent research reveals that AI adoption poses specific risks to human-intensive skills through what Ferdman (2026) terms "capacity impoverishment." Unlike skill obsolescence in domains like hunting or basket-weaving, the deskilling of core human capacities diminishes us as humans and undermines our flourishing.

docs.title: Core Capacities at Risk
docs.text:
The following capacities are particularly vulnerable to AI-mediated deskilling:

  • Epistemic capacities: Theoretical rationality (thinking, considering reasons, forming beliefs) and practical rationality (phronesis or wisdom)
  • Social capacities: Moral capacity and abilities for developing meaningful relationships
  • Creative capacity: Making unfamiliar combinations of familiar ideas
  • Volitional capacity: The ability to exert effort, overcome difficulty, and persevere

These capacities differ from technical skills because they are constitutive of human flourishing. As Ferdman explains, "the deskilling of our core human capacities is bad because inadequate development of these capacities can lead to 'capacity impoverishment,' which, in turn, diminishes us as humans."

docs.title: Structural Dimensions of Deskilling
docs.text:
Deskilling is not merely an individual responsibility issue. AI creates systemic conditions that inhibit capacity development through:

  • Capacity-hostile environments: That restrict action possibilities for capacity cultivation
  • Undermined habituation: Short-circuiting the gradual process of skill development
  • Reduced intersubjectivity: Diminishing opportunities for shared valuing of capacities
  • Disembodiment: Limiting physical presence necessary for certain capacities

For market research professionals, this means AI tools that automate data interpretation without preserving opportunities for researchers to develop critical thinking may ultimately undermine the quality of insights produced.

docs.title: Evidence of Deskilling
docs.text:
Studies show AI dependence leads to: - Erosion of critical thinking (Bonicalzi et al. 2023) - Decline in decision-making and analytical reasoning (Zhai et al. 2024) - Reduced activity awareness and competence maintenance (Rinta-Kahila et al. 2023)

docs.title: Burning Glass Institute: Beyond the Binary
Overview
docs.text: Published in January 2026 by the [[burning-glass-institute]], "Beyond the Binary" represents a landmark analysis challenging the conventional wisdom that AI will either automate or augment jobs. Instead, the research demonstrates that automation and augmentation are frequently occurring simultaneously within the same occupations.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text: The study analyzed labor-market data from millions of job postings across 759 occupations, developing metrics to measure both automation exposure (tasks AI can perform) and augmentation exposure (tasks where AI enhances human capabilities).

docs.title: Correlation of Automation and Augmentation
docs.text:
• Exposure to automation and augmentation is strongly positively correlated across occupations
  • Jobs most exposed to automation are also highly exposed to augmentation
  • This finding validates the "automation-augmentation paradox" first identified by Raisch & Krakowski (2021)

docs.title: Skill Demand Shifts
docs.text:
• Automation-exposed skills were 16% more likely to see demand decline compared to baseline skills
  • Augmentation-exposed skills were 7% more likely to see demand increase
  • This creates a net shift in the composition of work rather than simple job elimination

docs.title: The Entry-Level Challenge
docs.text: The report identifies a critical concern: junior workers traditionally built expertise through foundational tasks (drafting reports, conducting research, building models) that AI can now perform or accelerate. This threatens established apprenticeship models and expertise development pathways.

docs.title: Real-World Examples
docs.text:
• Project managers see routine scheduling automated while strategic coordination becomes more valuable
  • Analysts spend less time producing first-pass models but more time interpreting and communicating implications
  • Consultants can produce drafts instantly but face higher premium on the quality of underlying thinking

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: The study concludes that AI is not neatly dividing the labor market but is changing the composition of work inside jobs. Organizations risk "automating the developmental tasks before they have redesigned the learning pathway," potentially gaining short-term efficiency while weakening their future talent base.
