docs.title: Avigail Ferdman's 2026 Paper: AI Deskilling as a Structural Problem
Overview
docs.text: Published in ai-society (2026) 41:3001–3013, this landmark theoretical paper presents a structural analysis of how AI systems undermine human capacities through systemic environmental conditions rather than individual failings. Ferdman argues that deskilling should be understood as a societal problem requiring structural solutions, not merely an individual responsibility issue.

docs.title: Capacity-Hostile vs. Capacity-Conducive Environments
docs.text: Ferdman introduces the critical distinction between: - Capacity-hostile environments: Systems that restrict, limit, or create a narrow field of affordances for capacity development, affording only shallow skilling while restricting fuller development of capacities - Capacity-conducive environments: Systems that actively encourage capacity development through rich opportunities for embodied interaction and shared valuing

docs.title: Philosophical Framework
docs.text: The paper constructs a capacity-skill framework showing that: - Being capacity-skilled requires agential control over human capacities - Capacity cultivation occurs through habituation - a gradual process of inculcation through attunement to individual cases - Habituation depends on intersubjectivity (learning from others who share the value of the skill) and embodiment (physical presence in social interaction)

docs.title: AI's Structural Impact
docs.text: Ferdman demonstrates how AI systems can create capacity-hostile environments by: - Automating routine tasks that deprive users of opportunities to practice judgment and strengthen 'cognitive musculature' - Encouraging plan-following rather than plan-forming, reducing users' agential control over life decisions - Creating disembodied interactions that undermine moral attention and relationship formation - Offloading critical activities to non-human agents, diminishing opportunities for capacity exercise

docs.title: Artificial Personal Assistants Case Study
docs.text: The paper analyzes how AI-powered personal assistants (like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini) can become capacity-hostile when users over-rely on them for life-planning. While APAs offer convenience, they risk: - Replacing self-deliberation with automated recommendations - Diminishing practical wisdom development by removing real-world experience - Narrowing the field of affordances for independent planning - Undermining intersubjective habituation through reduced human interaction

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text: This structural perspective explains why the entry-level-squeeze occurs - AI automation of foundational research tasks creates environments hostile to the habituation process required for developing professional expertise. The paper provides the philosophical foundation for understanding the human-operating-model-gap as a systemic issue rather than individual skill deficiency.

New tasks added to AI-exposed roles since 2022 are 2.5 times more likely to rely on human-intensive capabilities like empathy and creativity, quantified through the epoch-score (Figure 10). The report identifies a pronounced 'superstar effect' where the top 20% of AI-exposed companies achieve 5 times higher productivity growth (163% average) than the most exposed companies as a whole (33.5% in 2025) (Figure 12). Wage premiums for AI skills average 62% across sectors, ranging from 118% in Consumer Markets to 16% in Government (Figure 15). AI specialist job postings are growing eight times faster than total job postings, with Technology, Media and Telecoms leading at 11.4% of sector roles (Figure 16). These findings, derived from PwC's pwc-ai-occupational-exposure-index, demonstrate AI's asymmetric impact on labor markets and validate the ai-job-future-framework's predictive power.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: A comprehensive analysis of how AI adoption affects employment patterns across 21,559 U.S. firms, using observed AI spending data linked to workforce records. Published June 30, 2026 by Ara Kharazian (Ramp), Lisa Simon (Revelio Labs), and Ryan Stevens (Ramp).

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
• Linked Ramp's line-item spending data (identifying payments to AI vendors) with Revelio Labs' workforce records
  • Defined AI adoption as the first month of a three-consecutive-month spell where AI spend is at least $100 monthly
  • Measured adoption intensity as monthly AI spend per employee (PEPM) over first three months after adoption
  • Used Callaway-Sant'Anna framework for staggered treatment timing
  • Compared high-intensity adopters (top PEPM tercile) vs. low-intensity adopters (bottom two PEPM terciles)

docs.title: Key Findings
docs.text:
• High-intensity AI adopters grew employment by 10.2% following adoption
  • Entry-level headcount rose 12.0% for high-intensity adopters
  • Employment gains were broad across roles: engineering (+7.3%), sales (+10.3%), administration (+7.8%), customer service (+6.3%)
  • Gains emerged gradually, following what appears to be a "learning curve" as firms integrated AI tools
  • AI adoption is highly selected - adopters are larger, more technical, faster-growing firms
  • Early employment gains are concentrated in Information sector (13.4% growth for high-intensity adopters)
  • Low-intensity adopters showed no statistically significant change in employment

docs.title: Methodological Innovations
docs.text:
• First study to combine observed firm-level AI spending with workforce records at scale
  • Introduced PEPM (AI spend per employee) metric to measure adoption intensity
  • Addressed selection bias by comparing early adopters to later adopters in the same intensity group
  • Provided evidence against the prediction that AI adoption will lead to broad job losses
